He explains that the bill, which Congress disapproved regarding FCC rules on protecting customer privacy for broadband and telecom services, will eventually be signed by Donald Trump, who has approved it. He notes that these open service rules previously placed internet access services in the same legal category as phone companies, making them subject to long-standing privacy principles. He clarifies that while many rules were still being drafted, this new bill will halt that process, remove existing negotiated protections, and make it easier for corporations to track and profit from personal information, which could then be released through hacks, citing the Yahoo hack of 500 million accounts as an example. He also mentions that activists, including Fight for the Future campaign director Evan Greer, are concerned that gutting these rules will enable mass government surveillance and undermine cybersecurity, making personal information vulnerable to hackers, identity thieves, and foreign governments, which might sound like going too far.

So, this is a very different kind of an fight, and we have to fight it with a lot of strategy. And when we just heard the numbers, 7 lakh people die in India because of cancer, I was looking at that number in a totally different way. Supposing someone tells me that 17 flights are going to take off from Delhi..."
A man speaks, "every day. And each one of those..."

That's exactly the number of people we are losing every year because of cancer. 17 flights, not one day, every day of 365 days. That's the reason it's very important for us to reconcile that this is a battle has to be fought at three different levels. One is a level of us talking about as a nation, as a society, second, physicians and scientists, but it can also be fought at a level of an individual who can do certain things to really control this. And that's where I'll take that in US rates are very high but majority of patients they survive and I don't think it's because of anything else other than attitude."

A person speaks, "towards looking for it. This cancer one day was just about 1,000 cells. At that time it was totally could have been beaten up very easily by a minimal amount of zapping or a surgery or a medicine. But if we allow it to become trillion cells, then it becomes a totally different kind of a fight. So we have to bring the fight early on and only challenges at the time when it is treatable." This is followed by a cough.
A man speaks, saying, "doesn't produce any symptoms. So if we are waiting for symptoms."

A man speaks: "to come, we are letting the enemy win. So that's my strategy towards treating the cancer is to we have to set up our mind that don't expect symptoms. A man says, "could be prevented just by lifestyle changes."

A man speaks, "if we look at smoking, if we look at tobacco, if we look at fat and if we look at sugar and look at HPV and all those things, we can really stop 30% of the cancer mortality in India." Another man then says, "we've we've spent a lot of time initially by for treating cancer by focusing on the cancer cell itself. What we've come to appreciate is that cancer doesn't live in isolation, that the cells that the normal cells that surround the cancer in fact determine whether or not a cancer develops. And an important component of that is is the immune system. And when we realize that every cancer because it depends on mutations, there's a host immune response against those mutations, so-called neoantigens. A man speaks in a clear voice, "through antibodies, for example, uh, that unleashes the immune system against the cancer cells and is able to achieve very durable responses."

A man speaks, "And those have now been achieved in a whole range of cancers including starting off with melanoma but also lung cancer, head and neck cancer, gastric cancer, renal cancer, certain lymphomas and has transformed the way we treat cancer simply because these allow for a very durable response against against cancers without need for ongoing therapy in many cases."
A person speaks, "second other kind second kind of therapy that has also become."

A person speaks, "that's called commonly called CAR T cells. Um and these these therapies have already received FDA approval for treating certain kinds of leukemias and lymphomas."

A man speaks, "but are also likely to be tested in the future in solid tumors and other kinds of cancers as well. So there's a fairly and this is just sort of the tip of the iceberg. I think there's a general appreciation now that the the most one of the most effective ways of treating cancer is not going to be chemotherapy, but perhaps immune-based approaches that allow for a more durable and controlled response. Cancer after all is a setting where uh the the tumor cells learn to evolve over a long period of time. So you need a equally smart system. audio_captions: A woman speaks in a clear, professional voice, "How much money is your doctor taking from prescription drug companies? A new online database shows you how much pharmaceutical companies are paying Tampa Bay doctors and what they're paying them for. It is legal, but is it ethical? Tonight I'll show you how that database works and what you can learn from it."
A female voice says, "Dr. James, so" amidst background chatter.
A woman says, "Kaski heads up pediatrics at".
A voice says, "Florida Hospital Tampa," accompanied by a sustained electronic tone.
A female voice says, "He says doctors making money on the side for big pharmaceutical companies is nothing new, but it's on the rise," followed by a male voice saying, "doctor."

A man says, "are feeling the crunch because of the government cutting back on reimbursement. So they're looking at ways to supplement their income. Pharmaceutical firms are looking for ways to get more use of their drugs so they can make more profit. And so the two are obviously coming together here and filling each other's needs." A woman then says, "It's legal, but Orlowski questions if it's always ethical."

A man speaks, "Everybody, if you're just taking a drug that's already been researched and approved and you're adding more and more patients to the drug to see if it works or not, that's really not a real legitimate use of time or money." This is followed by the sound of a typewriter, and then a woman's voice says, "Dr. Jay Wolfson, a professor of medicine and public health."
A person speaks, saying, "that the University of South Florida."
A female voice speaks, "says the federal government is now mandating that".
A woman speaks in a clear voice, "pharm companies disclose what they pay to who and why."

A man speaks, "so that you and I and everyone else can go online to ProPublica and put the name of their physician in and find out if that physician receives any money from any pharmaceutical company for anything. Either lecturing, providing a scientific base for conducting studies, writing articles..." This is followed by the sound of keyboard typing. A woman then says, "According..."
A person speaks, saying, "to propublica.org," followed by a low buzzing sound.
A female voice says, "the website that holds the Dollars for Docs database." A whooshing sound effect plays, and the voice continues, "Florida is ranked..."
A female voice says, "second in the nation with over 168 million in payments."

A character speaks, "made to practitioners and institutions in 2012. Among the doctors in our area being paid a large sum of money." This is followed by the sound of paper rustling. The character continues, "Dr. Maria Carmen Wilson. According to ProPublica data, she received over $90,000 in 2012 for expert-led panels, business meals."

A keyboard clicking sound is heard as a woman speaks, "travel and educational programs from both Allergan and Eli Lilly. By email, Dr. Carmen Wilson told me in 2010 and 2011, she turned over about 140,000 in earnings to USF and the TGH Foundation. And she added, quote, 'I am one of the few physicians that sees Medicaid and county patients. My prescriptions for Eli Lilly are way below my prescriptions for generics.' Wolfson says, 'Most of the time doctors are doing legitimate research or education, but..." A man then says, "patients have a right to know if their physician is being influenced in any way by any outside potentially economic source that could encourage them to prescribe a drug or to use a device or to go to a hospital or to do anything that may not be in the patient's absolute best interest." The woman continues, "And apparently even doctors who are being paid by big companies are now expressing some concern. Dr. Selim Benbadis, director of the Comprehensive Epilepsy Program at the University of South Florida and Tampa General Hospital, got 117,000 from UCB, a company that makes epilepsy drugs, and believes it can be done ethically. But in published medical journals, he's expressed a concern about whether physicians who get paid to speak about a therapy should be forced to use only slides provided by the pharmaceutical company, saying, quote, 'I would never go in front of my peers and recite a slide deck. Slide decks are for sales reps. If the drug companies do nothing about this, they will lose all reputable speakers.'"
A person speaks, "Now, if you'd like to link to a website where you can check your doctor, head over to my Facebook fan page. Just search for Linda Rotado, WFTV."

Another woman follows, speaking, "Irene McCormack Jackson is one of 19 women who made accusations against Filner. 10 News reporter Melissa Mecia."

Another woman follows up, speaking, "Bill and Virginia, that news conference started about 30 minutes ago that we are streaming live on tennews.com happening here in the Westin behind me here in downtown. Irene McCormick Jackson was Filner's communications director, and again, she is walking away from this with a $250,000 settlement, saying that it is fitting that this settlement came right before election day. A woman speaks, "here from the news conference just a few minutes ago where McCormick Jackson that said that she is happy to bring this chapter of her life to a close. As a part of the agreement, McCormick Jackson will leave her employment with the city on April 1st and each side here will pay its own attorney fees. Another woman speaks, "It was really scary to go public about how the former mayor sexually harassed me. I didn't know what to expect. I remember walking back to my office afterward, my eyes on the ground and my shoulders hunched. I cringed when people recognized me and waved me down or called my name. But I was wrong. To all the women that I met in the elevators, at sandwich shops, at baseball games, on the beach, in the grocery store, in my neighborhood, at the nail salon, on a hike, or even at a rest stop in Central California, your thanks meant the world to me when I just wanted to be reclusive."

A woman with a clear voice speaks, "Of course, this is a difficult situation for her and all the women involved. Now, the city attorney did say that it was cheaper and less grueling to settle this case rather than take it to trial. Again, that news conference still ongoing. I'm going to run back up there, see a new information and bring you that coming up here at 11:30. Reporting live in downtown, Melissa Mesihah, 10 News." Another person says, "Thank you Mel, meantime..."
A woman says, "And news is on top of a breaking story in Fallbrook where reports..." accompanied by background music.

audio_captions: A female voice speaks, "in a port in Bandar Abbas in Iran. Still no word from the crew. The Stena Impero stays put. Audios now emerged appearing to reveal that Britain's warship nearby, HMS Montrose, tried to intervene."

A man speaks with a radio-like quality accompanied by static, "You obey, you will be safe. If you obey, you will you will be safe. Alter your course to 360 degrees immediately. Over." A woman speaks, "Then the Iranians contact HMS Montrose to make clear the message is not directed at them." The first man speaks again over the radio static, "Foxtrot 236, this is Sepah navy patrol boat. No challenge is intended. No challenge is intended. I want to inspect the ship for security reason. Over." Another man speaks with a radio-like quality, "Sepah navy patrol boat, this is British warship Foxtrot 236. You must not impair, impede, obstruct, or hamper the passage of the MV Stena Impero. Please confirm that you are not intending to violate international law by unlawfully attempting to board the MV Stena Impero." The woman speaks again, "That confirmation never came. Pictures released by".
A person speaks, saying, "State media show Iran's revolution."
A person speaks, "regard boarding the ship. They say it was breaking international maritime law," accompanied by a low rumbling sound.
A female voice speaks, "Earlier this month, Britain was involved in capturing an Iranian oil tanker suspected of carrying..."
A female voice speaks, "oil to Syria which would be a breach of EU sanctions."
A woman says, "Now questions are being asked about why Britain wasn't more prepared for retaliation."

A man speaks in an assertive tone, "I understand, and I understand this from reasonable sources, that Washington had offered the UK government, even in the event that they haven't quite agreed an allied position to this, to use US assets to support British shipping, and they were not taken up at the point. And I want to know why. This is a major failure, and the government has to answer this charge very quickly indeed."
A female voice speaks, "The government has condemned Iran's actions."
A woman speaks in a reporting tone, "It's broader policy seems unclear, wary of a..."
A female voice speaks, "aligning itself too closely with President Trump's more confrontational stance."
A woman asks, "worried that the US and Iran could be heading for a military conflict." A man responds, "I think everybody."

A man speaks, "...worried about that, which is why the Foreign Secretary, the Defence Secretary as well, is wanting to make sure that we de-escalate. We have seen, as I say, a ratcheting up in the last three weeks of events and tensions in the Straits of Hormuz and with Iran as a whole. We need to make sure that we thwart this, go back to the bigger picture of the relationship with Iran, and make sure that we protect our international shipping."
A female voice says, "In a tweet today, the Iranian ambassador to Britain warned against the UK escalating tension, calling it dangerous and unwise."
A person speaks, "This evening, Iranian TV are running pictures of the detained ship. They say the crew have been taken off for questioning."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "in a clear message. The oil tanker captured for flying a British flag now flies an Iranian one." A second woman then speaks, also in a clear voice, "Aisha reporting there. We're joining me now is Alistair Burt, who was a foreign minister until earlier this year. Mr. Burt, you will have heard Ian Duncan Smith say that the US had offered assets to support British ships in this volatile region and the UK re..."
A female voice speaks, "rejected it. He says it's a major failure of government. Do you agree with that?"

A man speaks, "I'm afraid I don't know the background that Ian Duncan Smith is talking about. Uh, I've not, I've not been involved with this, so, uh, I don't know to what he's referring. I'm quite sure that will be the subject of the statement that Jeremy Hunt will be making tomorrow in the House of Commons, when I'm sure he will be questioned about this, but he will set out the United Kingdom's position in relation to this, uh, and what we're seeking to do to de-escalate the tensions in the Gulf." This is accompanied by the sound of birds chirping. A woman then says, "Um..."
A speaker says, "We only had one ship in the area ourselves, is that..."
A character speaks, "a major failure of government," followed by a musical jingle.

A man with an English accent speaks, "Well of course only the previous week, the UK had been able to intervene in order to prevent a ship being seized. There's no doubt that the security of vessels in the Gulf is now a major international issue, not just for the UK but for everyone else. And it's obviously going to be absolutely vital that ships are able to use that passage of water freely and safely. And I suspect it will call for something like an escort system or something similar. This cannot be produced overnight, it does take time, but it's essential that we give a clear message that ships should be free to move. If they are impeded, there will be a serious likelihood of an international incident. And it's in the interest both of Iran and of the other states who use the Gulf that we get this issue of maritime security sorted out. But you cannot also divorce it from the wider issue between the United States and Iran and the other issues that are going on in the Gulf. This is a symptom rather than a cause, but a very nasty one."
A person speaks, saying, "points to a very difficult dilemma facing the new Prime Minister and."
A person speaks, saying, "days away of course. They now have a difficult decision to make. Do they stick with the Europeans?"
A woman speaks, "The French and Germans trying to keep the Iran nuclear deal alive."
A woman speaks, "to they align themselves with Donald Trump and a much more aggressive stance. What would your advice be?"

A man speaks in a clear, formal voice, "My advice would be to stick to our independent course, that is to make our judgments on what we consider to be right. The nuclear deal was a was a really important diplomatic milestone. Iran conceded quite a bit by agreeing to the JCPOA. And the fact that it's been abandoned by the United States, albeit for reasons we understand because of other issues concerning Iran, doesn't help anyone trying to get a new negotiation and a new agreement started. I think we're right with other European partners to try and keep Iran from moving back towards acquiring a nuclear weapon. That cannot be in anyone's best interest. But equally, the concerns expressed by the United States are not minimal. Iran has got to realize that it will not be able to deal with this matter merely by asking everybody else to do something and redress what it considers to be its grievances. It must do something as well. But there must be more talking and more negotiations rather than a move towards any other form of confrontation."
A woman speaks, "already today it will be an early test of diplomatic dexterity."
A woman speaks, "Well, step forward Boris Johnson." A man responds, "Yes." The woman continues, "Does that calm your..."
A female voice says, "nerves will give you a breakdown."

A man with a clear voice speaks, "I know that the British Prime Minister guided by the very best quality of diplomats and support in the Foreign and Commonwealth Office will always be able to display diplomatic dexterity, independence from others, and I'm quite sure whoever occupies Downing Street after Tuesday will be able to demonstrate that."

audio_captions: A person speaks, "Family and friends gathered in grief tonight to remember a young man murdered at a Family Dollar store in Dearborn. They're also very worried about his co-worker who's been missing since that happened."

A man says, "is news reporter Sheryl Choden standing by live in Dearborn Heights tonight and I imagine a lot of heavy hearts there, Sheryl." A woman replies, "Absolutely, Stephen, heavy hearts and total disbelief. This young man was murdered at a job that he was proud of and had for only one week." Another woman's voice is heard saying, "They lit candles and said prayers as they comforted one another."
A person speaks, "and cried over the loss of their friend Joe Orlando, the 20-year-old who was murdered where he worked at the Family Dollar store in Dearborn."
A female voice says, "I mean you see stuff about this everywhere else, but not like somebody that you know. So it's like crazy," accompanied by the sound of background chatter.
A character speaks in a solemn voice, "I love that man. That was my best friend. That was my brother." This is accompanied by background music.
A woman speaks in a clear, reporting tone, "His assistant manager, Brenna Machus, also 20, is missing tonight. Police fear she could be in danger."
A female voice speaks, "As family and friends of Joe gathered at the vigil outside the church school where he went as a young boy, they remembered Joe with fond stories."
A person says, "... and they raised their children."
A female voice speaks, "high in the air, desperate for some answers."

A woman speaks through tears, "He was such a good person. As you can see, he's got friends, he's got family. We all love him very much. And we'd do anything for him. And for him to just be gone... You know, a week at work. Like somebody please come and help. Somebody come up and say something because this is somebody that we love." Sounds of sobbing and the indistinct murmur of a crowd are audible.
A woman speaks, "Earlier today, the families of both Joe and Brenna talked to reporters."
A man speaks in an emotional, choked-up voice, "He's got his life together. He got the job on Thursday at Family Dollar."
Sounds of crying accompany a person speaking in an emotional voice: "He was so happy... There are so many people that need Brenna, and we love her and miss her and we want her home."
A woman speaks in a somber tone, "She's a loving friend, a loving daughter, niece, in-law, cousin. Anybody and everybody that knows her needs her back in her life."

A woman with a crisp voice speaks, "Hearts broken tonight for sure, and so much concern over Brenna. If you know anything, of course, call the Dearborn Police. In Dearborn Heights, I'm Cheryl Choden."

A female voice says, "Channel 7 Action News." A male voice follows, speaking, "Cheryl, thank you. Such a tragedy to report on tonight, but as you mentioned, there is a reward out for information, $11,100 tonight. That's the information to help find Brenna Machus. Crime Stoppers also announced there is a $2,500 reward which would lead to the arrest of this suspect. So if you know anything about this crime, call 1-800-SPEAK-UP. You can remain anonymous."

audio_captions: A subtle electronic jingle plays before a woman speaks, "Wall Street cares about trade. Today's session proved it. Stocks moved higher when the U.S., Canada, and Mexico reached an agreement on steel and aluminum tariffs. But then stocks headed in the other direction on reports that talks between the U.S. and China have stalled, leading to concerns of retaliation, which could hit global growth. Kayla Tausche starts us off tonight in Washington." A brief musical transition sound plays, followed by another woman speaking, "In the Trump administration's multi-faceted trade fight, progress on two fronts, stalling on the other."

A woman speaks in a clear, professional tone, "Today brought news that the White House would lift steel and aluminum tariffs on Canada and Mexico, two close U.S. allies whose support President Trump needs for the new NAFTA."
A man speaks, "So that deal is going to be a fantastic deal for our country, and hopefully Congress will approve the USMCA quickly."
A female voice says, "Today's deal lifts tariffs in the..."

A woman speaks, "next 48 hours. It ends retaliation against U.S. products like beer kegs, whiskey and pork and drops bitter lawsuits over those actions in hopes of clearing a path for the trade agreement. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau expressed confidence." A man then speaks, "Now that we've had a full lift on these tariffs, we are going to work with the United States on timing for ratification, but we're very optimistic we're going to be able to move forward." This is accompanied by background chatter.
A female voice says, "The White House shelving another set of tariffs, this time on automobiles." This is accompanied by background humming.
A female speaker says, "with a decision delayed up to six months."
A female speaker says, "while it negotiates with Europe and Japan."
A female voice says, "But Trump hasn't ruled out those charges entirely."
A man speaks, "and they take advantage of us on trade. It's not, it's not fair. We lost 180 billion dollars with the European Union."

A female voice speaks, "Republican lawmakers who have sought to persuade the president against tariffs sounded their support. In a statement, Nebraska Senator Ben Sasse said, quote, 'China is our adversary. Canada and Mexico are our friends.' The president is right to increase pressure on China. He's also right to be de-escalating tension with our North American allies. In what Sasse called the 'Cold War with China,' sources say talks have stalled, as Washington and Beijing double down on their positions and discussions over the next round of talks in flux until they can agree on what they will talk about. For Nightly Business Report, I'm Kayla Tausche in Washington."

A person speaks, "I'm hoping that with that being said..." This is accompanied by the sound of city traffic.

A person asks, "Are you considering running, or are you running, or..."
A woman speaks: "I'm definitely running. I am on the ballot for November. And yes, it's way out of my lane and league."

A woman speaks, "and it may not always benefit you personally."

audio_captions: Upbeat, rhythmic music plays. A woman speaks, "Welcome back to The Real Story. Donald Trump's campaign manager Cory Lewandowski now facing misdemeanor battery charges in the state of Florida. So it stems from that confrontation that you can see on the screen there with a reporter. In new surveillance video now, Florida police releasing this tape appears to show Lewandowski grabbing the arm of former Breitbart news reporter Michelle Fields as she tried to ask Trump a question. She has since resigned from Breitbart along with some former colleagues claiming the organization failed to support her. Trump issued a statement in support of Lewandowski today and says he will plead not guilty. Joining me now is Kurt Bardella, former Breitbart spokesperson who was among those who resigned a couple of weeks ago. Kurt, great to have you back on The Real Stories. So, what do you make of the developments today? Well..."
A person speaks, "It just shows what we've known for a very long time, which is Donald Trump and Corey Lewandowski are essentially pathological liars."

A man speaks, saying, "they said when this happened, it didn't happen. They said that there was no physical contact made. They said that perhaps the person was making it up, all of which has beyond a shadow of a doubt proven to be not true. And now when confronted with the evidence that's pretty black and white footage, surveillance that shows that there was a confrontation, it got physical, that what indeed Michelle said happened, really did happen, they're still walking away from it and not accepting responsibility. And it's real insight for the country to see exactly what kind of president Donald Trump is going to be and it would..."

A man asks, "point is the is the line drawn where enough is enough. How far do do things have to go before someone like Donald Trump accepts responsibility for what the closest advisor in his own inner circle does? How long before we see some accountability?" A woman replies, "Well, it's interesting because we just had a Cruz spokesperson on who after that incident happened with their spokesperson, different, totally different kind of incident, they fired Rick Tyler. Uh, so they did have some action. Uh, Trump doubling down today as we've been reporting and saying that uh, Lewandowski is a decent man in a tweet and that nothing happened in the video. And also, Kurt, I want to draw your attention to what Trump said back on March 10th, the day or two after the alleged incident. Here it is."

Amidst the sounds of a crowd, a man says, "The Secret Service are amazing people. The Secret Service are amazing people, they said absolutely nothing happened. He didn't hear about it until like the next day. So, I wasn't involved in it, but the Secret Service was surrounding everybody, and they said nothing happened. Everybody said nothing happened. Perhaps she made the story up. I think that's what happened." A woman repeats, "Perhaps she made the story up. I think that that's what happened," and then asks, "What do you think about that?" A second man answers, "Well, I think at the very least, Donald Trump has a responsibility as a leading presidential candidate to directly apologize to Michelle Fields for throwing out that reckless and point-blank untrue assertion that this has been made up. Regardless of the legality of what assault is or isn't, the reality is something happened, it's proven beyond a reasonable doubt that it did. The statements that Donald Trump has verbally made about this whole thing are completely untrue. They've been proven..."

A male speaker says, "untrue and he needs to do the right thing and step up and accept responsibility for it and apologize. There's a big concern right now that this is just going to be a broader indicative of what we can expect from Donald Trump as the leading Republican presidential candidate and as potentially the commander-in-chief, and it's completely unbecoming of someone who wants to be president." A female speaker then says, "You know, it's really interesting, Kurt, because there's, you know, always two sides to a story and when this first came out and you couldn't really..."

A woman speaks in a clear voice: "you see exactly what happened, you know, people were very vociferous on both sides of the aisle saying, 'Hey, she made it up, it didn't happen, whatever.' Well, now if you look at the police report, it says this, it says on March 12th, I obtained video footage from Trump's security at Trump National in Jupiter. I specifically obtained video from the ballroom that night and time in question. The video parallels what Fields had told me. Lewandowski grabbed Fields' left arm with his right hand causing her to turn and step back, etc. This is from the police officer. Now everyone gets their justice."
A female voice speaks, "in court, and we have no idea what Corey Lewandowski is going to do, no contest or"

A female voice speaks, "plead not guilty, I guess, according to Trump. But now it's official and there's a charge." A male voice then says, "Well, and I think that's again one of the real troubling things to me."
A man speaks, "is the observation that the the evidence existed that Donald Trump was willing to go out there, make public declarative statements with no wiggle room."

A man speaks, "knowing that this evidence existed and either didn't have the fortitude to look at it himself or didn't care enough about the truth and decided to go out there and say what was in his opinion politically advantageous. And again, that is a dangerous mindset from someone who wants to be the commander-in-chief of this country. And what kind of message are we sending."

A man says, "to people, to women in this country, to children, that it's okay to do whatever you want, that it's okay to solve, resolve conflicts through physical intimidation, through violence, through putting your hands on somebody and not accept responsibility for that. It's a very, very slippery slope and there's going to be a broader impact that this is going to have if it's allowed to continue." Then, a woman speaks, "Kurt Bardella, great to get your thoughts today. Thank you."

audio_captions: A female speaker asks, "So talk to us about the investigation of proteins. Why is it lagged? Why is it so important?" A male speaker replies, "Thanks, Caroline. Well, so normally".

A male speaker says, "is building a new platform to comprehensively and quickly measure proteins in a sample. And proteins are important because all of your cells in your body, and there's 37 trillion roughly in an average human." A brief hum is heard. He continues, "Your cells are made of proteins and proteins do all of the work in your body. Over the last couple of decades, humanity has made it easy to measure DNA in a sample, like a drop of blood. For example, I could take a drop of blood from you, I could analyze it in a couple of days for less than a thousand dollars, I'll have 99% of your DNA. The breakthrough that enabled that has never occurred for proteins. The analog, if I take that same drop of blood and I want to know what proteins are in that sample, the best we can do as humanity after spending weeks and tens of thousands of dollars is get to approximately 8% identification of what's in the sample. And that has broad implications across therapeutic development, precision medicine, and has really hampered the delivery of this personalized medicine wave that we've been talking about for the last few decades." A female speaker then says, "So, why has it been left behind? Is it just incredibly difficult? What, you're putting money to work, you're wanting to get people involved, partners are interested, but how hard is it going to be to get more than 8%?" The male speaker replies, "That's a really interesting question. And I think one of the things I think would be really interes."

A male speaker with a clear voice says, "and talk about is that the way that humanity conquered the genome is by borrowing some of the processes from nature. Nature already has processes to copy and read DNA. Those are necessary for cell division. And with that, we are able to take DNA from a sample and amplify it so that you can make a bright enough signal that you can read. For proteins, once something becomes a protein in your body, it can never be copied or read back. And so the technology required to read it is quite difficult and approaches have been very slow to develop. About five years ago, my co-founder Parag Malik, who's Stanford faculty, came up with a very unique idea which is really an idea rooted at the intersection of computing, data science and biochemistry to bring a novel approach to not just measuring 8% or 10% of the proteins in a sample, but measuring comprehensively 95% of the proteins in a sample." A female speaker follows, saying, "I mean, what's been so amazing about"

A woman speaks: "out 2020 is how we've seen suddenly biotech take reach center stage. The decade of investment that we saw in mRNA in, you know, what we now see as CRISPR developments has really helped us have breakthroughs when it comes to the vaccine race that we've seen upon our hands. But what in terms of investing in knowing our proteins, what's that going to lead to, do you think? Can push us forward 5, 10 years?" A man responds: "Yeah, that's a great question, Caroline. I think..."

A man speaks in a calm, measured voice: "that, you know, we should celebrate the enormous accomplishment that the scientific community has delivered with MRNA vaccines and with the response to the COVID-19 pandemic. One of the sad truths though is over the course of the last couple of decades, the rate of new drugs being approved by the FDA has not significantly increased. And during that two-decade period, the spend in research and development in pharmaceutical companies has nearly quadrupled. And if you look at what's going on today, Biopharma has picked off many of the easy drugs for common ailments. And they need much more information that they can apply machine learning and deep learning to to be able to figure out what are the differences between healthy and sick cells? How do I build a better therapeutic? And the promise of the technology that we're working to bring to the world is that you'll be able to build better therapeutics in less time with higher efficacy and less toxicity." A woman with a crisp voice speaks: "We're looking at a chart of your share price because you recently went public via a special purpose acquisition company, the good old SPAC. Why? What's it done for you?" The man responds: "Well, so I think to first and foremost, to understand why, you have to understand what are our motivations for going public. And, you know, I'm a former public company CEO. I know what it's like to be public and certainly there's a lot more scrutiny and a lot more work being a public company. But for us, the increased visibility of being a public company and the greater access to capital was really important. And it's important because our company has transitioned out of a phase of feasibility and research trying to figure out how we're going to solve the problems that need to be solved to bring this platform to the world. And now we've moved into a phase of formal development and manufacturing. And with that comes a lot of headcount growth, it comes a lot of expense growth, and being a public company aids us in a number of ways."

audio_captions: A man speaks, "When a tragedy occurs, it can be hard to talk to your child about what happened. How do you explain it? How much will he or she understand?" A woman continues, "Joining us this morning once again is parenting expert, Dr. Natasha Sharma with tips on helping your child cope. So good to see you." Another man says, "Thank you very much for joining us today. Difficult time for parents right now trying to explain what's been going on." The woman then says, "As an expert and as a mom of two yourself, here we are again. It was just a few months ago when you were here talking about the Yonge Street van attack and how do we broach this topic? So what do you recommend this time?" Another woman begins to speak, "Well, you know, because..."

A woman speaks in a calm, measured voice: "There's a few events that have occurred in such a short span of time that we can get this sort of false sense of insecurity around our safety. And I think I still maintain that with younger kids, it's best not to bring it up. You know, the really little ones, sort of under eight or so. If they haven't brought it up themselves, I wouldn't bring it up with them. With teenagers and older kids, they might know something about it. They probably will. So you could ask them about it, you know, you could say, 'Have you heard about this, yes or no? How do you feel about it? And is there anything you want to talk about?' But I would sort of, you know, keep younger kids away from any graphic news footage, and be just really careful about projecting some of our own reactions to this onto them."

A man speaks, "How do you how do you if they don't want to talk about it, what do you let it go at that point? I have a 10-year-old son and he is like he's a boy. And so how do you how do you get him to how do you get them to either respond or do you just let it go?" A woman replies, "I I think let it go."

A person speaks: "I mean, if they seem to be distressed after they don't want to talk about it, and that could look like um a child who whose mood has changed or they're getting, you know, more withdrawn than usual, so they don't want to go outside or they seem to be more afraid to go out in public and do their usual things. You know, no one should feel unsafe, especially still in this city. Um we don't want to get this idea that we can't go out about and do our normal routine and enjoy the public the way we always have. So if you have a child who's expressing fear of doing that, then then you might have to sort of go in a little deeper. But if, you know, for example, if your son doesn't want to talk about it, I wouldn't push it. Just say, okay, it's it's okay to not have um a"
A female voice says, "strong emotional reaction to it as well for children." Another female voice then says, "Or let's say if it's manifest its way itself."

A woman speaks, "ways like tummy aches or maybe they're not sleeping properly. If they don't want to talk about it, can you still say something to allay their fears without going through the actual events that unfolded?" Another woman replies, "Yeah, I think if you."

A woman speaks, "you see behaviors in your child that seem unusual or different than their usual self. So, you know, if they're sleeping or eating differently or if they're just feeling sicker than usual, they don't want to go to school or outside all of a sudden, then you know, you might have to broach that topic with them or just maybe ask them, it's better to ask an open-ended question. You you don't seem like yourself, you know, you're you're is there something bothering you? You can talk to me about it and see if they'll open up about it." A man begins to speak, saying, "And".

A man speaks, "in locations because these are very public locations. If your kids are worried about going to those areas, what can you do to try and allay those fears?" A woman responds, "You know, we live in sort of this climate where..."

A woman speaks: "There's so much bad news and fake news and so much access to news and it it's we have this overrepresentation of the negative. So, you know, with that psychologically we can get this again, that false sense of of not being very safe. So I think it's very helpful to remind ourselves that the chances of something like this happening to any one of us, um, certainly in this city in most parts of of this continent is really rare. So I think it's important to remind our children and ourselves of that, that this is, you know, we should continue to enjoy our lives in the very same way we did before this unfortunate event. And you can focus..."

A woman speaks, "So on the good. I love that you say you can make them helpers and thank the helpers." Another woman responds with an affirmative "Mhm." The first woman then asks, "So how so?" before the second woman begins to answer, "Well, you know..."

A woman speaks: "When things like this happen, what's interesting to see or maybe not so surprising is that people will step up. You know, my favorite part of of the radio, as I was talking about earlier, is the feel-good moment of the day where they talk about the good stories, and we just don't get enough of that. And you know, when when things like this happen, it's remarkable to see how many people who are there, standing by or passerby or just people who were around them, rush to the aid or just anything that they can do. People really do step up."

A woman says, "and I think it's good to also place focus and emphasis on that remind people that there's a lot of good in the world." A man responds, "And we saw that on Sunday night. We were talking about that yesterday, the number of people who who risked their risked their own lives to help people out. It was incredible." A woman adds, "They were amazing."
A woman says, "Yeah. Yeah. Absolutely," followed by a man saying, "Great advice. Thank you so much."

A male voice states, "Jeff Fager, the executive producer of the oldest and most successful news magazine program in history, 60 Minutes, was fired this afternoon by CBS News."

The ticking of a stopwatch is heard as a male voice speaks: "And in its more than 50 years on air, only two people have led that broadcast. Fager succeeded the show's creator, Don Hewitt, in 2004. Fager also recently served as the chairman of the CBS News division."
A man speaks in a calm voice, "when we cover a story and report it on Sunday night and it has impact on Monday morning, that's what you hope for."
A male speaker says, "Fager hired Charlie Rose for multiple roles at the network. In November, Rose was terminated."

A man speaks, "July, six female former CBS News employees told The New Yorker Fager would touch employees in ways that made them uncomfortable after drinking at office parties. Nineteen current and former employees told The New Yorker Fager allowed harassment in the division. Fager vehemently denied all of those claims. Fager continued to come to work. On Sunday, The New Yorker reported a new accuser said she felt compelled to speak because she simply can't believe Fager's back there. The article described her as a producer who was an intern at CBS in the early 2000s who said that he groped her at a work party. A background shout of, "Twice sir, left..." is heard. A man says, "Baker's departure comes days after CBS Chairman and CEO Leslie Moonves resigned following allegations of sexual assault and harassment."
A man says, "CBS News President David Rhodes today briefed the 60 Minutes staff."
A male voice says, "Can't talk to you guys about uh, about this today." This is accompanied by the sound of city traffic.

A man speaks in a clear, reporting voice, "In a statement, Rhodes said Fager's dismissal was not directly related to the allegations surfaced in press reports, which continue to be investigated independently. However, he violated company policy and it is our commitment to uphold those policies at every level. Fager said in his own statement that CBS terminated my contract early because I sent a text message to one of our own CBS reporters demanding that she be fair in covering the story. My language was harsh. CBS did not like it." This is followed by a musical chord.
A man speaks in a clear, narrative voice, "That reporter was CBS correspondent Jericka Duncan, who said today she wanted to be transparent about it."

He went on to say, 'Be careful. There are people who lost their jobs trying to harm me, and if you pass on these damaging claims without your own reporting to back them up, that will become a serious problem.'"

audio_captions: A woman speaks: "Well, back to news from the pitch now. South Africa's national under-20 squad has just left for the FIFA World Cup in South Korea with one goal in mind, to do the African continent proud. The Amajita are in group D alongside Japan, Uruguay and Italy, and maintain they aren't at the tournament just to make up the numbers. CGTN's Sias du Plessis has more from Johannesburg." A short musical sting plays.

A man speaks, "After months of preparations and a successful training camp in Europe, the South African under-20 team are finally on their way to the World Cup. The team is buzzing..." This is accompanied by background chatter and ambient noise.

excitement and eager to do the country and continent proud. For Braga B striker, Luther Singh, it's a moment all footballers dream of. Well, every footballer wants to go to a World Cup regardless of what age group it is, but for me, I think I'm grateful and I'm on, it's a big opportunity for me to go to the World Cup. It's a dream come true for me, even if it's under 20 level, but I'm still grateful for it and I'm very excited to play for.
The sound of people murmuring is followed by a male voice speaking, "Head coach Tab says that preparations have been satisfactory and that".
A man says, "squad is well prepared to show why they are a force to be reckoned with at the tournament." Another man says, "We're not going there to add numbers."

A person speaks, "Uh, we are looking to compete, we are looking to get a respectable position, but yeah, let's take one game at a time and not put any pressure on the boys. Let's allow these young boys to enjoy the every match."
A man speaks, "Let's allow these boys to enjoy the moment." Another man follows, "The under-20 Afcon top scorer says he is not focusing too much on."
A person speaks, "...a gold tally for the tournament. Instead, he is concentrating on..."
A person speaks, "...magita to the next stage of the football showpiece," accompanied by the sound of a crowd.

A man speaks, "I mean, this tournament, it's it's a big tournament, but then I'm not putting pressure on myself. I just play the same football I played and I'm just taking the same thing that I took with me when I went to the AFCON and when I went to COSAFA, so I'm not putting any pressure under myself. I'm just going there to do what I know I can do best and to help the team in a way."

A male speaker says, "Sinong's men have set their sights firmly on the group stages of the tournament. The confidence is high, the talent in the squad is certainly capable of progressing from what is indeed a tricky group. A woman with a clear voice speaks, "Florida's Governor Rick Scott is slamming the federal government, saying that the Zika antibody tests and lab support that he requested has not come through. Meanwhile, the Department of Health and Human Services has sent Congress a letter saying there is an urgent need for them to pass 1.9 billion dollars in funding to combat Zika."

A woman speaks, "Congress is on its seven-week recess until September 6th." Upbeat, rhythmic music begins to play as she continues, "Joining me now is the Secretary of Health and Human Services, Sylvia Mathews Burwell, who wrote that letter."

A woman speaks, saying, "Madam Secretary, thank you very much. I think you're sort of caught in the middle here. So we're doing everything we can. We've moved and have access for the governor to 35 million dollars to do the work that they need to do. Additionally, I think folks know we've sent an emergency response team in to work with the governor's team on the ground in terms of investigating these cases and making sure that that mosquito control is done. A woman speaks, "having the funds to manage this issue as we need to do and as the American people deserve. And that's why we've written the letter and that's why I'm very hopeful that when the Congress gets back in September, that they will very quickly move the funding that will allow us to keep our vaccine research going, which is one of the most important solutions to the Zika problem for our nation, as well as making sure that we have the resources that if there are other cases of local transmission like there are in Florida, that we are able to support other states and other places in their efforts to combat it." Another woman asks, "And do you have concerns for instance about the Gulf Coast where the flooding, the incredible flooding, devastating Louisiana is going to lead to more breeding and more mosquitoes there?" The first woman replies, "You know, with regard to the mosquito."

A woman speaks, "in that entire Gulf area. That's a group of states that we focused on from the very beginning. Another woman responds, "Now, before I let you go, I want to ask you about the pharmaceutical company Mylan that produces those EpiPens. A man speaks, "paying very close attention to the race here. President Obama has been declared the winner in your state of of Rhode Island. No surprise there." A woman corrects him, "Delaware," followed by laughter. The man continues, "That's right, Delaware, excuse me. A man speaks, "You know, I mean, I'm I'm obviously encouraged. I mean, I see a number of the states, uh the president seems to be uh leading. Um, doesn't surprise me. A man speaks, "you know, what what Mitch McConnell said a few years ago, uh which is that their number one priority is to uh make the President a one-term President. It's it's so important for the business community that they deal with the fiscal cliff. The uncertainty is is a huge challenge. And uh I think they'll they'll hopefully recognize that people want a balanced approach to actually deal with this." A woman then says, "Now we should"

Two men speak. The first man says, "point out that you won your race tonight with more than 70% of the vote. Congratulations. Uh, and your Democratic uh Senator Tom Carper also uh won election. Uh so a couple of Democratic wins there in uh Delaware. What are you seeing in the Senate races? Because the Senate is obviously going to be critical to this equation going forward." The second man replies, "Uh, it is. And I'm uh I haven't seen the latest uh yet tonight, but I'm encouraged there as well. Uh and and frankly in part because I think the Republicans uh across the country did what uh Delaware Republicans did a couple years ago when they nominated, when they uh selected Christine O'Donnell uh instead of Mike Castle. The first man then says, "Yeah, and."

A man speaks, "and of course there've been some significant Republican losses. Olympia Snowe's seat in Maine has gone to an independent, Angus King, who's expected to caucus with the Democrats. A third voice also says, "Right." There is faint background chatter.

A man speaks, "I think uh, so you know, we could have a similar situation to what we had before and so it's going to come down to uh uh the work that uh, you know, Speaker Boehner does with his uh with his caucus. I mean I think the American people clearly said in this election that they expect uh Democrats and Republicans to work together to deal with some of these really uh huge issues that the country is facing." A man speaks in a clear voice, saying, "very much, uh, Delaware governor, Jack Markell. Thanks for being with us."

audio_captions: Upbeat electronic music plays, followed by a woman speaking: "Breaking news. Uh, just as fire crews have made a dent in the monster Woolsey fire, it exploded again with a flare-up near Lake Sherwood. It quickly grew to 1,000 acres. Here is the latest. That fire is now estimated at 96,314 acres. It is only 35% contained. The full containment estimate has been pushed back from Thursday to Sunday. The fire has destroyed at least 435 structures; 57,000 are still in its potential path. Let's go live to Stu Mondel in Sky 9. Stu, what can you tell us?" A man then begins speaking, accompanied by the sound of a helicopter's rotating blades: "Well, we know that this flare-up happened earlier this afternoon. Still a lot of smoke and a lot of activity out there at the Woolsey fire. We can see this. We're actually making our way out there right now in Sky 9. I can tell you we're over Simi Valley looking out towards the Hidden Hills area, and it gives you an idea how big that smoke plume is. Now, it does look like it is just cresting to the top of that hillside right there. We do know fire fire crews and firefighters have been on this all afternoon. They're trying to get that fire out, and of course, they are trying to keep those structures safe. We understand in that area, though, there are no structures in immediate danger. But I can tell you after all that fire activity, the folks that are down there in the Ventura area and also in the Westlake Village area, they're probably not happy seeing that huge plume of smoke, and of course, the other side that's over there in Malibu. Right now, though, they are working to get these that these flames contained as this hotspot still continues to burn. Live in Sky 9 over the Simi Valley area, I'm Stu Mondel, back to you guys in the studio." The woman replies, "All right, Stu, thanks for that. KCAL9's Riley..."
A male speaker says, "Paige is live in Lakeshorewood where there were some very tense moments today. Randy?"

The sound of a helicopter whirring is heard. A man speaks, "There were one. I'm going to get out of the way so you can see this amazing sight. We've been watching the helicopters filling up here at Lake Sherwood all day long non-stop. This has been an incredibly important resource because that flare-up you're talking about happened so close to here. Take a look."
A man speaks, "This flank of the fire blew up at about 9:15 this morning," accompanied by a low whirring sound.
A person speaks, "You can see the strength of the wind by the shape of the smoke," accompanied by the sound of wind blowing.
A man speaks, "It's almost horizontal as it races up the walls of the canyon." This is accompanied by a low rumbling sound.
A man says, "The air attack was fierce for at least four hours."
A male commentator speaks, "with plenty of resources available to join the fight."
The sound of a large, heavy vehicle moving, followed by a single musical chord.
The sound of helicopter rotors is heard as a male voice speaks, "water-dropping helicopters were able to fill up and be back on the fire within minutes at Lake Sherwood."

A male voice speaks, "because the flare-up was so close here along the ridge line on a peak called Boney Mountain. At this point, the wind was blowing the fire away from homes, and firefighters wanted to knock it down before it had a chance to change its mind. Firefighters weren't the only ones caught..." This is accompanied by the sound of wind blowing.
A man speaks, "by surprise when the fire blew up without warning. One former LA City firefighter who's lived in the Lake Sherwood area for 30 years was impressed by what he saw."
A male speaker says, "Most of this area was burned like uh five to ten years ago. So um, I'm optimistic that they can keep it out of the houses in this area."
A male voice says, "Alan Tyser came from Newbury Park to watch the aerial ballet."

A male voice speaks, "I'm very familiar with the area and I was here during the last big fire, so I come out to perimeter here, check out the smoke, watch the activity, marvel at the... the bravery of our firefighters." This is accompanied by a low rumbling sound.

A helicopter whirs. A man says, "And as you see that massive Erickson Skycrane now, just finished taking a load of water. It's going to be moving up, and I want to show you how close that flare-up was. It's still going, and how close it is to our location, right up there on the ridge top. They'll be hitting it, continuing to hit it as they try to knock that thing down and make sure it does not threaten homes here. Let's go back to you." Another man replies, "Let's hope it doesn't happen. All right, thanks so much, Randy."

audio_captions: A woman speaks, "Today, lawyers for Michelle Carter went before the state's highest court to argue she should have never been convicted of encouraging her boyfriend's suicide." A man then speaks, "WBZ's Adam Myler was at the court for the hearing."

A woman speaks, "This case made national headlines when Michelle Carter was found guilty of involuntary manslaughter for encouraging her boyfriend to commit suicide. Today Carter's attorneys took the case here to the Supreme Judicial Court, hoping to overturn her conviction." This is accompanied by background city noise.

A woman speaks in a crisp, clear voice, "Michelle Carter was not in the courtroom today as her lawyers argued that the now 22-year-old should not have been found guilty of involuntary manslaughter for the suicide death of her boyfriend Conrad Roy when they were both teenagers. Last year, Carter was sent..."
A woman speaks, "sentenced to serve 15 months behind bars, but she is still..."
A female voice speaks, "...free pending this appeal before the Supreme Judicial Court," accompanied by the background murmur of voices.
A female speaker says, "was accused of sending dozens of text messages encouraging her boyfriend to kill himself. Roy was found".
A clear female voice speaks, "dead in his truck of carbon monoxide poisoning back in 2014."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "Prosecutors said Carter was on the phone with him while his truck filled with toxic gas, but she never called 911. They also said at one point he got scared and got out of the truck, but Carter told him to get back in."
A woman speaks, "I think that there's a lot of evidence that she expected him to die at that point," followed by a buzzer sound.

A male voice speaks, "There's no evidence that ever actually happened, except for a message she sends, one of hundreds of messages she sends, only one of which makes that claim, that she sends months after. We don't convict people based on uncorroborated confession." A low hum is audible in the background.

A woman speaks: "It will likely take months for the Supreme Judicial Court to issue a ruling moving forward. The defense says they are keeping all their options open. Reporting in Boston, Anna Meiler, WBZ News."

Good Day's Paul Millican is live there this morning. And Paul, there's nothing more patriotic than a nice big breakfast." A man responds, "You got it, absolutely. We are..." This is all accompanied by the murmur of a crowd.

The sounds of a bustling restaurant, with background chatter and clattering dishes, are heard throughout. A man speaks, "showing our patriotism this morning, eating our eggs and our bacon and our French toast... at the White House restaurant." He interviews the owner about the restaurant's history and the atmosphere on election day. The owner says, "America is a great country. We can survive anything or anybody." Laughter is heard at several points during their conversation. The first man then announces the results of a "breakfast election," saying, "The winner is your breakfast president, French toast." He jokes with a woman that the loser was "Fruit and yogurt," adding, "Sorry healthy people, we're in the south right now. We want fried, we want breaded, we want sweet." The woman laughs and agrees, "Ain't that the truth."
A woman says, "have it hearty. I love that. Okay, French toast. Quick trivia for you. You get, I'm gonna give you two guesses. Who was president in '48?" A man replies, "Oh. Oh."

A male speaker says, "Jeez, I'm going to make a total fool of myself because I have absolutely no idea. I'm just going to throw out the name, let's see, I know it was it was it was after FDR." This is followed by a clattering sound. A female voice responds, "Ah." The male speaker continues, "Truman." Another male voice begins to ask, "Is that".

A woman speaks, "an hour?" A man replies, "I don't know." The woman says, "Okay, Truman. You did somebody tell you? Somebody told you." A man says, "Sure." The woman continues, "It was Truman." The man asks, "No, is that right?" The woman replies, "Yes." Laughter is heard as she adds, "You got it right." The man says, "I'm a genius. I do work for the White House, you know. Of course I know that." The woman says, "That's true. They're lucky to have you. They're lucky to have you. Paul, thank you so much." The man interjects, "I work for the White House." Laughter is heard again, and the woman says, "You better not come back empty-handed. He knows better than that."

audio_captions: A short, melodic, synthesized tune plays, followed by a man speaking, "Good evening, I'm Daniel Anthony. It's Thursday, the 13th of July, Harrison Ford's birthday. In response to Kelantan's amendments to the Sharia Criminal Procedure Enactment 2002, which now adds caning in public for certain offenses, Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said that the amendment should be seen in the context of it being applicable only to Muslims in the state and it did not involve non-Muslims." This is all accompanied by a rhythmic drum beat.
A male voice speaks, "Although the bill has been passed, it is still pending assent from the Kelantan Sultan before implementation," accompanied by rhythmic electronic music.

Rhythmic, upbeat music plays while a man speaks, "Meanwhile, Tourism Minister Nazri Abdul Aziz was confronted with a question about whether the new law would drive tourists away from the northern state. And this is what he had to say about it."

A male voice speaks, "dikenakan untuk orang Islam. Jadi kalau terpulanglah pada turis. Kalau tak nak pergi dia boleh pergi negeri lain. Lagi banyak lagi. Kuala Lumpur ada, Sabah, Sarawak lagi. They are more attractive to me."

Rhythmic, electronic background music plays as a male voice speaks, "An ultimatum issued by PPBM Deputy President Mukhriz Mahathir to Prime Minister Najib Razak to apologize for a statement about him lapsed yesterday afternoon, prompting Mukhriz to file an application for contempt today at the Kuala Lumpur High Court."

A person speaks, "This is over a statement that Mukhriz's father and Bersatu chairperson Dr. Mahathir Mohamad is seeking to safeguard his legacy with the hope of making his son, who is Mukhriz, the prime." This is accompanied by a soft, rhythmic electronic beat.

A man speaks in a clear, professional tone, "Minister. However, Justice Ahmad Zaidi ruled that the hearing of Mukhriz's suit against Tengku Sarifuddin, which has been fixed for today and tomorrow, would proceed first. He promised to hear the contempt application at the earliest date." This is accompanied by rhythmic electronic background music.

A person speaks, "After some radio silence, Penang-born 1MDB-linked businessman Jho Low finally speaks out. A spokesperson for the entrepreneur was quoted by The Malaysian Insight as saying that the attempts to link him to those who pleaded guilty in Singapore's 1MDB-related court cases were based on unfounded assumptions." This is accompanied by rhythmic background music.

A person speaks, "going as far as to say that the suits are an example of an overreach with a politically motivated act and selectively chosen narrative alleging 1MDB as a victim when it has been clearly stated by the Malaysian authorities that there has been no misappropriation of 1MDB funds." This is accompanied by rhythmic background music.
A male voice says, "Bloomberg yesterday quoted Singapore prosecutor Nathaniel Khun saying that the main victim in this case is 1MDB." This is accompanied by rhythmic electronic music.

A male voice speaks, "DAP veteran Lim Kit Siang wants Prime Minister Najib Razak to make like Singapore's Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and conduct a special three-day debate on 1MDB during this month's parliament sitting." This is all accompanied by light, rhythmic background music.
A man speaks, "He also suggested that parliamentary immunity should be waived for the session which he proposes should be held from the 24th." This is accompanied by rhythmic background music.
A person speaks the words, "the 26th of July. On top of that, he said that he would like Najib to..." over a light, rhythmic beat.

A male voice speaks over light background music, "Jho Low to be in attendance as well so that he can address the parliament and answer questions from MPs on the 1MDB scandal. He also asks if Jho Low is innocent of any grand larceny or billion-dollar money laundering, why has he disappeared from the public scene?"

A male voice speaks clearly, "And that's all we have today, ladies and gentlemen. For more stories, you know where to go. That's kinnytv.com. Do subscribe and share this video. I'm Daniel Anthony. Thank you for watching." This is accompanied by upbeat bass music.

audio_captions: The sound of applause is followed by a man speaking, "Delightful to be back here again."

A man speaks, "over the course of the last 30 or 35 years or so, I've spoken in this chamber maybe about 20 times. It's the first time I've ever done it when it's not been a debate. And it's the first time I've ever done it sober." His words are followed by a burst of laughter from an audience.
A crowd laughs, followed by a person speaking, "Uh, if anybody wants me to see..."

A man speaks, "speaking when I'm drunk. I am speaking in the debate tomorrow night. So please do, uh, so do come back and see if, uh, see if we can tell the difference." This is followed by audience laughter. He continues, "Um, it's also genuinely a privilege to be here because, uh, of the tremendous list of, of amazing people who have spoken here in the past. I'm looking at the, uh, bust of William Gladstone there, whom I'll say something in a moment. Last night we had John Bolton speaking here. Tonight, I came here through a demonstration against"

A man speaks, "Julian Assange. Last night, you had speaking here a war criminal who had a major part in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Iraq. And there wasn't a single demonstrator outside against him. Some of you have got your values seriously messed up." This is followed by applause from a crowd.
A crowd applauds, cheers, and whistles.

Sustained applause is heard. A man begins speaking: "I resigned from the British Foreign Office in which I was an ambassador because I came across the torture of people to get so-called intelligence and I came across extraordinary rendition. When I resigned, or was sacked, I don't care what you say..." The audience laughs, and the speaker continues, "Um... I was satisfied that I'd done the right thing. I had lost my career, I'd lost everything I'd worked for my whole life, but I could sleep at night. I knew that the intelligence gotten from torture was untrue because you don't get the truth from torture. Forget these stupid films about Bin Laden, forget 24, forget Hollywood. The vast majority of people tortured for intelligence are completely innocent. And the people doing the torture are the thugs of Mubarak, or the thugs of Karimov, or the thugs of whichever dictator is employing them. And they are not disinterested seekers after truth. They are people wanting to create the narrative their master wants to hear. And unfortunately, we had a period where in pursuit of war, Western intelligence agencies were knowingly accepting intelligence from torture in order to propound false narratives that pursued war. That is what we were up against. Why we need WikiLeaks and organizations like WikiLeaks, why we need whistleblowers is you can no longer automatically trust governments. I knew people personally, I'd worked with people, I knew people very, very well who were involved in the preparation of the dossier, the dirty dossier on Iraqi weapons of mass destruction. I actually happened to have had as a previous job being in charge of the FCO section monitoring Iraqi attempts at weapons procurement. I can tell you for certain that the majority of people involved in the preparation of that dossier knew it was not true."

A thudding sound is heard, followed by a man speaking in an echoing voice: "and produced it under political pressure and I can tell you I know of people who were in tears. I know of people who were near suicidal. I know of the pressures they put on people. I know what they do to people. When I came out and blew the whistle on extraordinary rendition and torture, I was accused of sexual allegations. I was accused of blackmailing visa applicants into sex, which is rape in another word. I was not guilty. I was not guilty. It took me years to clear my name and it was the most appalling thing that can happen to you and anybody who believes governments do not do that kind of thing to whistleblowers is naive."
A man says, "Let me tell you something more. The other reason we need organizations like WikiLeaks is that the space of debate has narrowed."

A person speaks, "Because the mainstream media no longer allows a wide area of debate. I said I would come back to Gladstone whose bust is there. While he was leader of the opposition in the 1880 general election, the Third Afghan War was in progress..." A cough is heard, and the person continues, "...and Gladstone in his Midlothian campaign made a speech in which he said, 'Our troops have have driven the wives and children of the Afghans into the snows of winter. If they resist, would you not do the same? It is no longer politically conceivable that any leader of the opposition in the United Kingdom would say of people fighting against British troops...'"

A man with an echoing voice speaks, "If they resist, would you not do the same? Can you imagine if any mainstream British politician said that those fighting British troops in Afghanistan might have some right on their side as we had invaded their country? Can you imagine the way they would be drowned out by our ultra-nationalist and militarist media which we have nowadays, that there is no longer space in our society for the kind of the debate that Gladstone used to enjoy. And that servile nationalist, uh, role played..." Light coughs can be heard in the background.

A man speaks, "by the media is a reason why we need to fight back using alternative media. One thing people always recall about WikiLeaks is the helicopter footage of the Reuters journalists being killed by an American military unit. One aspect people forget is that the families of those journalists had been told for years by the Pentagon that the Pentagon had no information on what had happened." A cough is then heard. The speaker continues, "That lying to grieving parents in order to protect criminal behavior is an example, just one example, of the kind of cruelty of government behavior that makes whistleblowing necessary."

A person speaks: "WikiLeaks exposed reporting on the corruption, the good American diplomatic reporting on the corruption in Tunisia, which helped spark the Arab revolution. WikiLeaks revealed to the people of Yemen that their president had deliberately agreed with the Americans."

A person speaks, "to put out but American bombing and drone raids were in fact terrorist suicide bombs. I could go on and on with so much information that WikiLeaks has given that has enriched the world, made the world a better place. If we could always trust governments, we would not need WikiLeaks. But we can't and we do."
The sound of a heart monitor beeping is accompanied by a low, ominous musical score that builds in intensity and crescendos dramatically.

audio_captions: Synthesized electronic music with a pulsing rhythm.
A woman speaks, "How often do you see that consumers are really victims of reckless lending? Out of every 10 people that come to you..."

A man speaks, "I'd say 70% of the customers that we speak to have not had a genuine change of circumstance but have just overborrowed, got into a debt spiral because the banks have consistently lent them more money than they could afford."

A woman speaks, "How much responsibility rests on the consumer? How much responsibility should you say the consumer should take?" A man replies, "It's a two-way street. You know, let's let's face it. You borrowed there's there's two schools of thought. You borrowed the money, you should have to pay it back."

A man speaks, "you know, and at the same time, with, you know, we can consider that we're constantly getting text messages, being told we can borrow more money, we're constantly being flaunted payday loans that say that we can."
A man says, "you can just get by," followed by a woman saying, "without proper financial assessment."
A person speaks, "Exactly," followed by the sound of a buzzer.

A woman speaks, "sitting down with the consumer and also verifying the information that the consumer gives you. What I find very distressing is that people will say they'll do a financial assessment and then they'll tell you, um, but uh put that in for put in 2,000 rand."

A female voice says, "for that. Could you 3,000 rand for groceries? I spend more than that." A male voice responds, "No, no, no, don't do that. Put that in there, put that in there, put that in there." Another male voice then says, "if they do that at all."
A male voice says, "Yeah, absolutely," followed by a female voice that says, "So you..."

A person speaks, "you find that there is perhaps a level of crookery in terms of the financial assessments being done. Not in reckless lending, but in when financial assessments are being done, I don't think that all creditors are above board in the information that they take down."

A male character speaks, "You're absolutely right, and we can say a little bit about the sum of consumers as well." This is followed by a female voice saying, "Mm-hmm." The male character continues, "But for the most part, you know, banks and creditors are driven by targets. Which means that the people on the sales floor need to get to their target and it's hard to maintain quality control levels across the board. So people get to get away with things that they shouldn't be able to get away with, which is why, you know, we really need to crack down on reckless lending and start and start showing people what's really going on."
A person speaks, "at National Debt Advisors, you would advise people to come to you before or after they get into arrears?"
A male voice says, "it's uh listen, if you know that you're going to be struggling financially, it's always best to, you know, get in front of the problem and sort it out straight away."
A man speaks, "But for the most part..."

A person speaks in a conversational tone: "nobody really wants to believe that they're struggling, you know? and we we we will see them after they start to struggle. What we don't want is for them to come and see us when they've been struggling for too long because then is really difficult to help them."
A woman speaks, "Do you think that reckless lending by creditors is going to come to an end anytime soon?"
A man speaks, "it's a it's very it's very poignant and important question."
A male voice speaks, "You know, it's the the the National Credit Act only took off five, six, five, six years ago." This is followed by a low buzzing sound.

A man speaks, "And debt counseling is only really finding its way now. Reckless lending is going on day day in, day out. You know, I I don't once once again, will the creditors make more money by continuing their current on their current track or will, you know, will they make more money by cleaning their act up? It's somebody somebody somebody's got to do something about it."

A woman speaks, "before we see any real change to the system." A man responds, "Absolutely." The woman continues, "And again, it's one thing, I'm always concerned that it's one thing to have rules and regulations and acts in place, but it's the implementation of those pieces of legislation which is so important. And if we don't implement that, if we don't implement..."
A person speaks, "the fines, if we don't implement the consequences, if we don't implement exactly what the act and the legislation says," followed by a short, melodic chime.
A person speaks, saying, "that is when once again consumers are going to find themselves at the short end of the stick." A short musical jingle plays.

A man with a clear voice speaks, "And the chain's only as strong as its weakest link. And if the people on the telephones who work for the creditors aren't being trained properly, if they're not being monitored properly, then, you know, it it's they then the whole system falls down."
A female voice speaks, "Thank you, Sebastian, for coming into the studio and we look forward to having you again," followed by a low-pitched organ chord.
A man speaks, "Thank you, Ms. Fica. It's a pleasure being here."
A female voice asks, "Are you a victim of reckless lending? If so, let us know. Perhaps we can help." This is accompanied by soft background music and followed by a short musical chime.
Energetic, synthesized music plays, ending with a resonant boom.
