audio_captions: Rhythmic background music plays, followed by a woman speaking, "The 19th International Istanbul Puppet Festival runs until Sunday in Istanbul. It aims to bring together the world's best and most colorful puppet shows and I have one of the people behind one of them with me now in the studio."
A female voice speaks, "The puppet and mascot specialist from Singapore."
A female speaker says, "Hello and thank you for joining us." A male speaker replies, "Hello, thank you for having me on your program."
A woman asks, "How are you enjoying the festival so far?" A man replies, "Well, this is my second time here."
A person speaks, "actually, and I think the festival is wonderful."
A man says, "...did a wonderful job organizing the festival and bringing people from all over the world that comes to Singapore to Istanbul." A woman then asks, "What drew you to Turkey?"
A female voice says, "bits and puppeteering to begin with." A male voice responds, "Well, I was a aircraft mechanic and I'm very"

A male speaker says, "interested in things that move and things that, you know, comes alive. So when uh growing up, you know, looking at at materials, looking at puppet shows, it really draws me because you can breathe life into something that is inanimate." He then says, "Yes." A female speaker says, "Well that's..."
A woman speaks, "... of uh puppet traditions around the world, and there's also new creativity and new shows developing. What are some of your..."
A female voice says, "favorites," followed by a male voice speaking, "Oh, of course, Jim Henson's Kermit the Frog is still one of the best and most."
A male voice says, "well-known ones." A female voice says, "Jim Henson's." The male voice continues, "Jim Henson's, yeah, committed fraud."
A person speaks, "Mhm. So tell us about your show that's at the festival right now, called Single."
A female voice says, "four streets." A male voice responds, "Mhm. Okay, the streets of Singapore is."

A man speaks: "basically introducing, uh, you know, what's happening in Singapore, uh, to the people that sees the show. So we bring them on a little tour along the streets of Singapore. First stop we went to Chinatown, and then we see, you know, a Chinese singer and an acrobat. And then I will bring them to, uh, Little India, and then we will see, uh, you know, the, uh, uh, uh, Bollywood dancers. And then after that, I showcase the different ethnic groups of Singapore." A woman makes an assenting "Mhm" sound and then asks, "Do you hope to encourage some unity in the".
A female voice says, "show because you have different ethnic groups and you have all these colors in the show." A male voice follows, saying, "Definitely. I mean, you know, uh..."

A man and a woman have a conversation. The man says, "this is a crazy world we live in, and using puppetry as the medium, and then showcasing all the different ethnic groups and how we can live together and be at peace with one another." The woman asks, "What goes into making puppets?" The man says, "or making a show?" The woman says, "Oh." The man continues, "Oh, a lot goes into making a puppet. You know, a lot of people think that puppetry is very simple, but actually it includes sculpting and molding, it includes makeup, includes hair, includes fashion, theatrics, you know, there's a lot of the fine arts that goes into making a really nice and good puppet." The woman says, "Right. Well, uh, we're hoping you can show us part of your show." The man replies, "Well, that would be my pleasure." The woman says, "Yes, please." The man asks, "Right, shall we?" The woman says, "Mhm." The man continues, "Okay, I'm going to introduce to you, all right, a very well-known personality. Of course, everybody knows him, and he's the king of rock and roll." The woman replies, "Of course." The man says, "All right, if you're ready."

A man speaks, "Get it Mr. Salman, here we go." A drum beat plays, followed by a man singing along to rock and roll music, "Threw a party in the county jail. The prison band was there and they began to wail. The band was jumpin' and the joint began to swing. You should have heard the knocked out jailbirds sing..."
A male voice sings "Everybody rockin'" over rock and roll music played on an electric guitar and drums.

A man sings the lyrics, "Everybody in the whole cell block was dancin' to the Jailhouse Rock. Spider Murphy played the tenor saxophone, Little Joe was blowin' on the slide trombone. The drummer boy from Illinois went crash, boom, bang. The whole rhythm sec..." This is set to upbeat rock and roll music with a prominent drum beat and electric guitar.

A male vocalist sings energetically, "...dancin' to the Jailhouse Rock. Everybody let's rock. Everybody let's rock. Everybody in the whole cell block was dancin' to the Jailhouse Rock." This is all accompanied by upbeat rock and roll music.

Rock and roll music plays, featuring a rhythmic percussive crack. A man sings, "Number 47 said to number three, you're the cutest jailbird I ever did see. I sure would be delighted with your company. Come on and do the jailhouse rock with me."
A male voice energetically sings, "Everybody let it roll! Everybody know who failed now," accompanied by loud rock music with a prominent electric guitar and drum beat.
Upbeat rock music plays with a male voice singing, "run run run run," followed by "one two three," and "my world."

A male voice sings the lyrics, "...sat on a block of stone. Over in a corner weeping all alone. The warden said, 'Hey, buddy, don't you be no square. If you can't find a partner..." This is accompanied by rock and roll music.
An energetic male voice sings along with upbeat rock and roll music, "...use a wooden chair and rock. Everybody let's rock. Everybody in old cell block..."

A male vocalist sings, "...dancin' to the jailhouse rock. Shifty Henry said to Bugs for heaven's sake, the ones looking out a chance to make a break. Bugsy turned to Shifty and he said, 'Nix, nix.' I wanna stick around and wanna get my..." The performance is set against a backdrop of upbeat rock music featuring drums and an electric guitar.
A male voice sings, "everybody let rock," accompanied by rock and roll music and the sound of a cheering crowd.

A male vocalist sings a rock and roll song. The lyrics include "who's in the jailhouse," and the repeating phrase "dancin' to the Jailhouse Rock," which is followed by "Rock, rock, rock, rock." This is accompanied by the sound of an electric guitar and drums.

An upbeat electronic dance song plays, featuring a male voice singing, "Pump up the jam, pump it up." A deeper male voice interjects with shouted phrases like, "Get your booty on the floor tonight" and "Make my day."

Rhythmic music is playing. A woman says, "That was a ton of fun. Thank you for joining us on Showcase." A man replies, "It's my pleasure." The woman says, "Thank you." The man responds, "Alright, thank you." This is followed by a dramatic musical sting with a driving beat.

audio_captions: A male speaker with a clear voice says, "Welcome to TYT interviews. And tonight I'm joined by Ro Khanna, who's running for Congress in California's 17th district. Ro?"
A man says, "Welcome to The Young Turks." Another man replies, "Thanks for having me on." The first man responds, "Pleasure to have you."
A man says, "I mean our secret was so simple, right? We invest in an infrastructure." Another person says, "Mm-hmm," and the first man continues, "and we invested in public colleges."

A man speaks, "and that paid off big time. And we're not making those simple investments now. And the the the question is why why aren't we doing the things that the rest of the world is copying as a state and as a country? We basically," followed by a clattering sound.

A person speaks, "had free markets where we believed also in strategic investment in infrastructure and education and giving people a shot, in helping industry in basic research and development and universities. And the platform sounds so clichéd because that's what built the middle class."
A person speaks, "America but yet we're straining. There has to be a recognition with those who have succeeded that look, no one is".

A man speaks in a measured voice, "saying that you're evil or you're causing harm. But you have benefited from the same trends that are creating dislocations. And if we don't address the structural inequities, then you're going to see the type of potential xenophobia, the type of anti-immigrant sentiment, the type of polarization that we face in our country. And so you have, we all have a social responsibility to say, how do we help those who haven't benefited from the trends that some of us have been fortunate to benefit from? And that's what this presidential debate ought to be about."

A person speaks, "Because the reality is we're in a very competitive environment. We're in a world where we're competing with machines and competing with other countries. And how the obligation, my aspiration is for Silicon Valley."

A man speaks in a thoughtful, conversational tone: "to say, not okay, what's good for Google or Facebook or Apple, but, you know, we have been such privileged beneficiaries of these trends. What is now our obligation to make sure that other people have some of these opportunities and some of the things that that we've had. And that that debate, and that debate in a bipartisan basis, because if you care about American competitiveness, and you care about American greatness, you ought to care about making sure people are adjusting to that structural change. I grew up, you know, I was born in Philadelphia. I was a bicentennial baby. I grew up idolizing our Constitution, the Declaration of Independence, the sense of a common American identity. And and and it seems like that is going to be the challenge for our generation. What is that common American identity going to look like, which is respectful, inclusive, diverse of faith, but still have some common American bond. And I think that that we're struggling with that because we've had such dramatic social change. So there is this story that all of us have, most of us have, of some form of immigration that drove us here, where we weren't part of the in-group, we weren't part of the successful group, and yet through sheer grit, hard work, resilience, we did that. It was the European story and now it's becoming the universal story. And if that becomes America in the 21st century and we figure out how to get the public debate right and we figure out the economic transition."
A male voice speaks, "probably going to create a society and a nation that is a bit unprecedented in human history and".
A man speaks, "That's American exceptionalism, right? That's American greatness. That's the Athens, the of the world. That's our legacy to the world."

audio_captions: A swishing sound occurs, followed by a man speaking. "Let me get your sense then of what the president was hinting at last night, Sheriff. Has he talked to you personally on the phone lately?" Another man replies, "No, he has not. And that's okay. Now, they they put uh a press thing out that there would be no mention of this at their rally. But knowing the president, he has guts and courage. And uh my gut told me he was going to do it." The first man continues, "All right. Uh that was a former Maricopa County uh Sheriff uh who was kind of saying what a lot of people had suspected and and indicating that Joe Arpaio uh is going to be pardoned by the President of the United States. It's just a matter of time. Maybe given what happened in Charlottesville, uh not around this time, and certainly not last night, even though the president did seem to hint at that. Uh but there are a lot of people wondering where where does this go. Arpaio telling me that he had no conversation immediately prior to the president's visit or any heads up that this was going to be done or that the president was going to say what he said last night. Uh but he wasn't surprised that the president said it. He opted again, he said, that not to come to last night's rally and that it would be a distraction and not good for the president. To Forbes publisher Rich Karlgaard, former senior advisor to the National Republican Senatorial Committee, Lanhee Chen, and Independent Women's Forum president, Carrie Lucas. All right. Um, let me let me get a handle on on what's going on here. Rich, one of the first things that comes to mind is whatever you think about whether uh, you know, Sheriff Joe Arpaio deserves a pardon or or whatever, uh the timing was bad, right? After Charlottesville to to issue one, right?" A third man says, "Well, it was good and bad."

A male speaker says, "it was good for his base, you know, 35, 40% of Americans support Trump and appear to always will support him. But to move legislative issues like tax cuts and tax reform across the finish line, he needs more than that. So I wish President Trump would go out and lobby for tax cuts and tax reform at a time when we're really desperate to get those." Another male speaker responds, "You know, it is a distraction to his point, Lenny. One of the things that even the sheriff said is that I didn't want to be that distraction and yet in the middle of the President's address last night, he talked about even risking a government shutdown to get the money to fund a border wall. What did you make of that?" A third male speaker replies, "Yeah, Neil, look, I agree completely. The focus really needs to be going into the fall. It's going to be a very busy time. There's going to be a ton of things that Congressional Republicans want to get done, whether it's tax reform or infrastructure. And I think, unfortunately, this issue is a distraction. And the more it's brought up proactively and preemptively, the more of an issue it becomes. So I agree completely, it's a distraction. I think the President is on firm ground when he talks about the economy and economic growth. He needs to come back to those messages." The second male speaker then says, "You know what I wonder about though, Carrie, is that time's a-wasting and whether it's this pardon or, it is another thing we're talking about in addition to what's going on now in Washington and now given the bad blood and the agita we've seen develop between Mitch McConnell and the president, is this yet another distraction?" A female speaker adds, "Well, absolutely. And I do think both the Congress and the president need a win and they need to show that they can make some real positive policy change. And I think tax reform is where that starts and the American people want it. I think there's almost a bipartisan, even Democrats know that our tax code has been incredibly counterproductive in terms of economic growth. We all want jobs, job creation. So I think there is time to move forward. They don't have to find the perfect tax bill. They have to get something done that lowers taxes and simplifies the tax code. And that has to be the focus of this fall." The second male speaker begins to speak again, "You know, guys, I was..."

A man speaks, "thinking of what having a share of here that the illegal crossings into the United States are down markedly, depending on which statistics you want to use, either from inauguration day or from election day, 40% or more along the border. Does the president get credit for that, and if that is the case, do we need to build a wall in the first place, rich, to reinforce that?" Another man replies, "Well, he certainly gets credit among his base. The question is whether he gets much credit."

A man speaks, "...outside of his base because to get tax reform and a lot of the things this panel's been talking about, he's going to need more than that 35 or 40%. He is going to need uh senators like uh McConnell and and House leader Paul Ryan. I mean, this is a time to time to come together. No, I don't think we need the wall. I think he's done an effective job." Another man then says, "You know, uh..."

A man speaks, "you could look at this and and say, 'All right, well, this it might be a justifiable pardon if it ever gets to that.' A lot of people feel that the sheriff was railroaded here. He's been deemed a racist. He says he was just doing his job going after illegals, and it it scared other sheriffs after the the feds were coming at them to do their job. Uh, but the the results are the results, and he said he he he brought up the results to really get a handle on illegal immigration in his county. Does that speak for itself or will this always be a stain whether pardoned or not?" Another man replies, "Uh, I think this is always going to continue to be an issue. Look, immigration."

A male speaker says, "it is a challenging issue for the Republican Party. It has been for several years already. And whether you take a tougher on immigration, whether it's legal or illegal immigration tone like the president has, or whether you're looking more in the reform angle as folks like Marco Rubio have. What you see in the Republican Party is this is a very, very divisive issue. It remains a divisive issue. So, if if we're going to move forward as a party in terms of getting things done looking toward the fall, it's going to be important for us to be able to arrive at least at at some healthy amount of uh of agreement on the issue. And to the extent that you rub salt in the wound, it's going to get harder and harder to do that. You know."

A man speaks in a serious tone, "now stepping back from Sheriff Joe Arpaio and and whether you call this a distraction or a legitimate issue and one that the president should address with a pardon. We do know that uh even the talk of the border wall thing was and risk of government shutdown was opposite from let alone what Mitch McConnell was saying that it wasn't going to happen. Uh there would be no government shutdown and the debt ceiling would be raised. But his own Treasury Secretary, uh Steve Mnuchin had indicated as much, the debt ceiling will be raised, there will be no government shutdown. You get a sense that they're not all on the same page." A woman responds, "Yeah, you know, there's obviously a lot of miscommunication."

A woman speaks, "and they do need to focus on this, but I think that we can uh that we can take, you know, some some hope um from this idea, these reports that at least on the the getting things on paper on moving forward on a tax reform bill, flushing out that those tax principles that were put out earlier in this summer, that that process is moving forward. And that's what we care about. A lot of this, you know, that we all know that the White House um has a little bit of a trouble with message discipline, uh so um and same with Congress. But I think, you know, what's important at the end of the day is getting a law in place, getting a tax reform bill that accomplishes what it needs to. And the good news is that that process seems to be moving forward and"

A man speaks, "always moving forward. They need a win here or if you're looking for tax relief and I look at this through the prism of someone who just says taxes as having a big impact on economy. We can argue over their size and who gets what, but I do think they're beneficial. But I am worried, Rich, that um, I don't think they're going to happen this year and you guys are closer to this than than I am. So you're the experts, I'm not, but as you know I read a prompter so that makes me qualified. So Rich what I'm wondering about is whether if it does get pushed off to next year, I'm just looking at the legislative timetable, then what?" Another man replies, "Then I think the 2018 elections might be a disaster for the Republicans if they..."

A person speaks, saying, "want to assure their majority rule in the House and the Senate, they better pass that thing and they better make it retroactive to January 1st." Another voice says, "They're not going to do that," followed by the first speaker continuing, "Because only if they do that are we going..."

A man speaks, "...to be entering 2018 with 3% plus GDP growth." Another voice says, "Yeah." The first speaker continues, "If they do that, they win. If they don't, they may lose. And you and I know that if the Republicans lose the House, it'll take about five minutes for the Democrats to impeach Trump on whatever charge they can come up with." A different man replies, "Five minutes is a little maybe 10. Maybe 10." A woman laughs. The second man continues, "Uh guys, I we have so much breaking news here. I do appreciate you're taking the time out of your busy schedule and rolling with all this breaking..."
A male voice speaks, "news. Excellent as always. Thank you."

audio_captions: A single, sustained musical note plays.
The sound of water bubbling is heard, followed by a male speaker who says, "When you dive on a coral reef, about a fifth of the coral species you see were first cataloged and named by John Veron."

A narrator speaks, "The godfather of coral has been diving and studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef since 1972 and is now one of the most vocal lobbyists for its protection." A splashing sound is heard.
A person speaks, "This year, a combination of climate change and the El Niño Pacific weather system have created the conditions for the worst coral bleaching in history. Well..."

A person speaks, "lots of coral, it look looks like this and you can see the upper surface is white and the under surface is still almost the normal color of the coral." This is accompanied by the sound of water lapping.

A man speaks, "So, it's always that upper surface that bleaches first. And this guy, if it doesn't bleach anymore, will probably recover. But the way things are looking here, I think uh all this coral over here will go this this white color. And um"
A male voice speaks, "That's the end of it. Once they expel all the algae, they die," accompanied by the sound of gently splashing water.
A male voice speaks, "Extreme heat has caused sea temperatures to..."
A male voice speaks, "is about 1 degree Celsius above normal over recent months."
A male voice speaks, "enough to cause bleaching on 95% of corals on the pristine northern reef."
A person speaks, "the US National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration".
A person speaks, "says this is now the world's third mass bleaching event since 1998. A pattern not seen in modern times." A piano chord plays.

A person says, "It's the El Niño years that are worse because that's when we get uh slightly higher sea temperatures and that's what's causing the trouble at the moment." The sound of wind is heard, along with footsteps on a gravelly surface.
A man speaks, "Australia's coral bleaching task force has declared the situation worse than two previous mass bleaching events in 1998 and 2002."

A male voice speaks, "Corals can regenerate over time if water quality and temperature conditions are supportive. But global warming is increasing the frequency of extreme heat events," accompanied by a low humming sound.

A man speaks, "and scientists are worried the reef's very survival is under threat." Another man says, "There is nothing at all to stop one El Niño from wiping out the Great Barrier Reef within months. That's the problem. If..."
A person speaks, "And El Niño can cause one reef to bleach," while tapping sounds are heard.
A person speaks, "then it can cause all reefs to bleach provided the weather conditions".
A person says, "not conducive to it. It's like Russian roulette," accompanied by clicking and tapping sounds.
A person says, "just has to wait for the right combination of temperature and light," accompanied by a clicking sound, and continues, "and then it's all going to happen."
A man speaks, "Maybe not next year, maybe not in 10 years time, but it will happen. It means absolute catastrophe if we lose coral reefs." The sound of wind blowing gently can be heard.
A person speaks, saying, "not just the loss of coral reefs themselves, but," followed by a low, sustained musical chord.

A man says, "Coral reefs are home for about a third of all marine species at some point in their life cycle. So, if we lose coral reefs, then a third of all marine species go with it. And when that happens, you've got a massive ecological catastrophe." His speech is accompanied by the sound of water sloshing. A second man then speaks, "Scientists say not enough is being done to curb greenhouse gas emissions despite the Paris agreement."
A man speaks, "which aims to keep global temperature rises below 2 degrees," accompanied by the sound of wind blowing.

audio_captions: A dramatic and percussive musical sting.

A male news anchor speaks, "And more breaking news coming in this time from Mizoram, a day before the Mizoram elections. A big controversy has broken out. A local body has written to the Mizoram Church and demanded support for Congress Chief Minister. Manipur based Kuki organization has written this letter to Mizo Church. Letter has urged church to support incumbent Chief Minister Lal Thanhawla and has cited the injustice to the Christians in this letter, which is seeking support for the Congress party. So after the Congress Muslim appeasement in Telangana and Madhya Pradesh was exposed, this time around, a day before the Mizoram votes, this is a massive controversy breaking out. The letter addressed to Reverend Lalliankhuma is clearly indicating that there needs to be support to the Congress party. Let's listen in to this reaction that we are picking up from Mizoram." This is followed by a dramatic, orchestral news theme. A second man speaks, "The Kuki organization based in Manipur has written a letter to the Mizoram Church, the Presbyterian Church of which you are also a member, to the moderator of the Presbyterian Church asking him to..."

A man speaks, "openly support you for being a Christian faithful. And what, how, what do you have to say regarding this? Because Himanta Biswa Sarma has to say, the BJP basically has to say that the Congress is frustrated and desperate, that they are seeking help from organizations which have no base in Mizoram." Another man replies, "I have not sought any help from any quarter whatsoever. The Kuki church leader is an elderly man, and they have experienced the, you know, what you call, bad treatment from the state government and from the central government as well, and from the neighboring people. And their only solace, their only hope for their survival belongs is in Mizoram, of which the leader happens to be Lalthanhawla." The first speaker asks, "So, how do you see this Kuki organization extending their support and writing an open letter to the Presbyterian church?" The second speaker says, "I'm very grateful to them for doing that." The first asks, "You are grateful to them?" The second replies, "Yes, of course. Why should not I?" The first speaker continues, "But the Presbyterian church here is distancing themselves and saying that they are not indulging in to into any political activities." The second speaker responds, "They don't do that. They don't indulge in politics. But, you see, when their religion is threatened, they should be alert." The first asks, "Do you think that the BJP is a threat to the" The second man answers, "Of course, of course. Otherwise, why should they declare Christmas Day as a good governance day, so that Christians cannot properly celebrate Christmas day?" A woman speaks, "Okay, look at the controversy that's breaking out now from Mizoram. And will the Congress party explain what really it is planning to do ahead of polls in Mizoram? And now Aniruddha is joining us from the epicenter. In fact, Aniruddha, help us understand what really is happening here. You know, in Madhya Pradesh and Telangana, they're going on a minority appeasement overdrive, and here they seem to be taking help from the church. This is something that is a very serious allegation against the Congress party as well." A man speaks over the sound of wind and city traffic, "Yes, Aditya, absolutely. In Mizoram, 95% of the entire population consists of Christian majority. And the Kuki church, particularly the Kuki organization writing to the Presbyterian church here in Mizoram, which have around 60% of the total population as its member, is not shocking, but indeed, it is a, it comes as shocking because instead of distancing themselves or instead of giving a clear explanation, the Congress party does, president of the Mizoram Congress, the the Chief Minister Lalthanhawla, has in fact thanked the Kuki organization. However, the church here is very clear. The church here, the Presbyterian church, we talked to Reverend Lalrinruanga, who to whom the letter was addressed, he has said that he didn't brought the letter into the consideration of the executive council and it was never discussed in the executive council. However, he said that he did took up the matter with his office bearers and after discussion."

A person speaks, "they decided that this letter needs not to be discussed in the executive council, but and and he also said that that is the very reason that he haven't written a reply to that letter to the Kuki organization which is based in Manipur and have written that letter. On the other hand, taking advantage of the letter written to Reverend R. Lalrinliana, the leader, the moderator of the Presbyterian Church, Chief Minister Lalthanhawla has given an entire political twist to this to this controversy surrounding the letter. And the Chief Minister tries to justify it by saying that the Kuki, who are Christians and are living in Manipur, have been neglected by the state government over there, which is the BJP. And that is the reason why they have extended their support to to to to to to the incumbent Chief Minister of Mizoram. But this this this entire..." Another voice says, "Alright, Anil. Thank you very much for getting us those..."

A man speaks in a quick, clear voice: "Actually, but we have more political reactions pouring in on that big story that is breaking on Republic. The Congress going on minority appeasement in Madhya Pradesh and Telangana."

A male speaker says, "in Mizoram, they are desperately begging before the church for votes. And this is the reaction we are picking up from Himanta Biswa Sarma." This is followed by dramatic, orchestral theme music with heavy drum beats.

A male speaker says, "I think this is again Congress this goes to actually this reflect that how nervous Congress is because normally in a democratic election, we do not we do not involve such temple monks. I think these these are basically the frustration in the Congress party. That is why they are procuring certain kinds of letters or any many other things they are trying to do. But I don't think that those things will will be of any use. Yesterday you have seen the kind of response Prime Minister has got in Aizawl street. So I think that goes to show that this kind of tricks will not be able to succeed." This is followed by a short musical outro.
Dramatic and sweeping orchestral music.

audio_captions: A brief musical sting is followed by a woman speaking, "Mike Flynn was forced out as President Trump's first national security advisor three and a half weeks into the start of the new administration. He didn't even make it a month. After he got forced out in scandal, you might remember that Mike Flynn retroactively registered with the federal government for having been a foreign agent. He had been paid, turns out, about half a million dollars by a foreign government, by the government of Turkey, while he was part of the Trump campaign. When he finally, months later, retroactively registered as having been a foreign agent during the campaign, that made some other things make sense. We had known, for example, that on election day, Mike Flynn had published a very strange, over-the-top op-ed in The Hill newspaper. It argued against a Turkish cleric who lives in the United States. He's a legal U.S. resident; he has a green card. Flynn's op-ed, again, published on election day, compared this Turkish guy to Osama bin Laden and said that..."

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "that the United States should definitely hand him over to Turkey. Now, the authoritarian government in Turkey blames this guy in the US for pretty much all of their problems. He's their universal boogie man. They blame him for an attempted coup back in 2016. They blame him for everything. So it was a little weird that somebody from the Trump campaign was arguing, yeah, hand him over. Give him to the Turks, right? But that was Mike Flynn. It was a little weird. Then it got weirder. There were reports in the Wall Street Journal that Mike Flynn had had meetings with officials from the Turkish government in late 2016, at which they discussed basically kidnapping that Turkish guy. Kidnapping him and flying him on a private jet to a Turkish prison island. For this scheme, Mike Flynn and his son would reportedly be paid as much as $15 million."

A woman speaks, "That was the little side project he was working on while he was on the Trump campaign before he became National Security advisor. Uh now, Flynn's lawyer has said those allegations are false. Then NBC News."

A woman with a clear voice speaks, "further reported that in the weeks following Trump's inauguration, after Flynn took office as National Security advisor, a request was made to the FBI to, hey, let's look into sending that cleric back to Turkey. That exiled cleric. He's got a green card to live in the United States. He's a legal permanent resident of this country. He has lived in Pennsylvania for 20 years. He lives in the Poconos. The US generally doesn't hand over political exiles who are legal permanent residents of this country, who are not known to have committed any crimes in this country. We don't usually hand over endangered exiles to authoritarian regimes who are demanding their return because they blame them for the sun rising. But this week, NBC News reports that the Trump administration, once again, is going"

A woman speaks, saying, "gone after this guy, trying to send this guy over to Turkey. Trump administration officials last month asked federal law enforcement agencies to examine legal ways of removing of removing exiled Turkish cleric Fethullah Gulen in an attempt to persuade Turkey's president to ease pressure on the Saudi government. The White House is looking for ways to placate Turkey over the murder of US journalist Jamal Khashoggi, according according to two senior US officials and two other people briefed on the requests. NBC continues, quote, 'career officials at the agencies pushed back on the White House requests.' As one senior US official described it, quote, 'at first there were eye rolls, but once they realized it was a serious request, the career guys were furious.'" The sound of paper rustling can be heard.

A woman speaks, "with somebody who knows how things are supposed to work inside the administration or inside any administration on an issue like this. He knows what normal looks like in a circumstance like this. David Laufman was a long time..."

A person speaks, "civil servant and prosecutor at the Department of Justice. In February, he resigned as the head of the Justice Department's Counter Intelligence section, Counter Intelligence and Export Control section. Mr. Laufman, thank you very much for being with us tonight. It's always a pleasure to have you here." Another person replies, "Good to be with you, Rachel."

A woman speaks, "So, um, one of the things I raised here was Mike Flynn registering retroactively, um, as a foreign agent, uh, around the time that he or after the time that he left the the the Trump administration. Um, but the other issue here is the question of this US Green card holder, this man who is a legal US resident." A soft throat-clearing sound occurs. The woman continues speaking, "Um, the government of Turkey has been demanding that he be handed over by the US to Turkey so they can go after him for lots of different things. How are issues like that usually handled as a matter of US law enforcement?" A man then begins to speak, "Well, a formal request for extradition."

A man speaks, "...by a foreign government would be put into a process that's well established within the Justice Department. Career officials within the Office of International Affairs and elsewhere within the department would evaluate the validity and legitimacy of the request, determine whether it in fact reflects a lawful charge under Turkish law, and then an assessment would be made of whether that same offense charged in Turkey is also an offense under US law because there has to be something called dual criminality in order for the United States to be in a position to extradite someone here to Turkey. That wouldn't be the end of the process though, if the individual could lodge something called a political offense claim, claiming that the request from Turkey is really politically motivated, then there are defenses that could be asserted to preclude extradition."

A woman speaks: "In terms of this particular cleric, it's been widely reported that there have been multiple reports from the Turkish government and multiple forms of pressure from the Turkish government that they really want to get their hands on him. They they want this, they want him to be extradited. And whether that's taken the taken the form of formal extradition requests or whether that's taken the form of political pressure and lobbying, I think depends on the account. But is this a specific person who the US government has has considered in the past in terms of this these Turkish requests and and and Turkish pressure and and that the US has in the past decided, no, he shouldn't be handed over?" A man replies: "Well, I think the reporting you described indicates that there already has..."

A man speaks, "occurred a careful vetting by Department of Justice officials, career officials who do this for a living, and an assessment made that there wasn't a sufficient grounds for extradition. And what appears now, if this new reporting is true, is that the White House is attempting to strong arm career officials at the department and elsewhere at other agencies into manufacturing grounds to remove Mr. Gülen to Turkey or elsewhere." This is followed by a woman saying, "That is."

A woman speaks, "absolutely what the reporting says. Um, if in fact this reporting is accurate, I just have to ask your assessment as somebody who's been there and who's dealt with these sort of things. Um, how big a how big a deal is this? I mean, how how unusual is this and how loudly would you expect people in the agencies, including the Justice Department, to squawk over this kind of pressure from the White House to reverse the decisions, reverse the views of career officials who work on these things as a professional matter." A man then says, "I I think it would be unusual if the facts as reported."

A man says, "were true. As I said, there's already been reportedly a very careful vetting of the validity of the Turkish government's request, and this is maybe not even a second bite of the apple but a third or fourth bite at the apple. And so it appears that they're just trying to create a pretext under some set of facts to eject Mr. Gülen out of the United States in order to placate the Erdoğan regime, to soothe its current hostility toward the Saudi government in order to appease a regime that our own intelligence community has alleged now has committed one of the grossest human rights atrocities in modern memory." A woman then says, "David Laufman, the former chief of the Justice Department's Counterintelligence and Export Control."
A female voice says, "it's always an honor to have you here, sir. Thank you very much for your time tonight." A male voice replies, "Thank you, Rachel."

A woman speaks in a serious and emphatic tone, saying, "the framing that Mr. Lochman just put on that there, I think just shouldn't be skipped over. I mean, what NBC is reporting here is that if you combine this with the new reporting from the Washington Post that the CIA says that the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia ordered the murder of this US journalist. Crown Prince orders that. US journalist gets murdered. Turkey raises the alarm about it and says, you know, we've got evidence that it happened. That happened on our soil, happened in our country. We think Saudi Arabia did it. Now the US is offering, what can we give you, Turkey, in order to make you stop making so much noise about what Saudi Arabia did here. How can we placate you and calm you down and quiet you down in your upset over what Saudi Arabia did here. Jamal Khashoggi was a US resident, worked for the freaking Washington Post. He was a US journalist. We ought to be the ones who somebody's trying to placate here. We shouldn't be, I mean, if you, right? If it's a, if the Saudis did this and if the CIA knows that the Saudis did this, we're trying to keep other people quiet from complaining about Saudi did this, doing this? And in doing so, we're maybe going to hand over somebody who we're pretty darn sure they're going to torture and kill once he gets there? What, what dystopian movie is this? We'll be right back." This is accompanied by the sound of rustling paper.

audio_captions: Upbeat, rhythmic music plays briefly. A woman speaks, "Well, we are here at the community barbecue to celebrate 100 years for Saskatoon Transit. What an amazing milestone, just one of the many centennials happening in our city. I am joined now by Bob Howe who is branch manager of Saskatoon Transit. You look incredible. 100 years. I heard you were the first branch manager." A man replies, "Well, the first branch manager who came from the driving ranks. Yes, I was. But and and thank you." The woman continues, "Ah! Really? I didn't even know that about you. You came from the driving ranks. So you were a driver for how long?" The man answers, "I drove for bus for about 15 years, then I moved into the supervisory ranks and worked in..." This is all accompanied by the sound of a crowd and indistinct chatter in the background.

A man speaks, "...for a bit and then was operations manager, access transit manager, and now I'm the transit manager." A woman replies, "Look at that. And I I'm taking you weren't quite driving the bus behind us, right? It was it was something a little newer?" The man states, "I actually have driven this bus several times in my uh in my previous career. Absolutely." The woman continues, "I'm just making age jokes and they're falling flat. It's it's not going well for me now. But you're always doing something great in the community. The last time I interviewed you, we were stuck on a bus, really, really cold, but you're doing something great. You're stuffing the bus full of food for the food bank. How did you even find time to celebrate this centennial this year? You guys are so busy." The man says, "We are very busy, but this is a monumental occasion. 100 years serving the city of Saskatoon and and transit has evolved so much from the from where it was and where it is and where we're..." Laughter is heard, along with background chatter and activity.
A male voice speaks, "going, so we're continually on the move and just having and enjoying ourselves in service."

A man's voice says, "...in the great city of Saskatoon." A woman replies, "Exactly. There there have been so many changes. I mean, 100 years, yes, but even the last five years there's been so much change. And looking ahead in the future, what are you guys looking forward to?" The man responds, "Looking forward to the future, we're looking at improving our transit amenities, making them more modern. We're looking at installing GPS on all of our buses and upgrading our software." This conversation is accompanied by the sounds of city ambiance.

A man speaks, "that people will be able to find out where the bus is in real time using their using their Android phones. So, yeah, it's uh, they're I'm sorry, using their smartphones. And uh, there there's so many things on the on the go for transit right now. We're looking at a new Civic operations center, a new transit facility because as we've been, you know, we've been in our present location for 100 years, it's time to move." A woman responds, "100 years. Yes, definitely. There are some great uh, new things on the horizon. Now, the other thing is that it it's been about 100 years since the idea for the Circle Drive South project first uh, came to fruition. And now next week it's opening. How excited are you as part of transit for that?" The first man answers, "Oh, we're very excited about that. That will change a lot of the traffic congestion that we've seen and uh, I think it'll go, it'll help us improve some of the routes that we want to use to service that area. Uh, it just opens up a whole new floodgate of opportunity for us." The woman says, "Okay, now coming up, we've already heard from folks here at the barbecue uh, just birthday messages for transit. Everyone's very positive and they're very uh, happy for your 100 years. Do you have a special message you'd like to share?" The man replies, "I just want to say, you know, thank you so much City of Saskatoon for everyone who uses transit or everyone who wants to use transit. Please come on out, give transit a try and we have bigger and better things coming in the future as well. So, thank you everyone for your support and your continued support." A second man then says, "Congratulations uh, Saskatoon Transit on your 100th birthday. It's been a pleasure working at transit." All of this is accompanied by the indistinct chatter of a crowd.

An older man speaks, "His name was Dick Ford and he drove from 1943 to 1982 he retired. And uh, happy birthday, Saskatoon Transit." He is followed by another man who says, "Congratulations and uh here's to 100 more." This is all accompanied by indistinct background chatter.

audio_captions: A short musical jingle plays. A female speaker says, "Madrid City Hall has seen a change of the guard in the last few weeks. The Spanish capital has a new mayor, Manuela Carmena. She's a member of Aura Madrid, a citizens' initiative backed by the..." This is accompanied by the sounds of a crowd and light applause.

A female speaker says, "left-wing Podemos party. Her priority is helping the less well-off in Spanish society, much like Greece's governing Syriza party. Marta Gomez, another member of our..." All of this is accompanied by the background sound of a crowd murmuring.
A female voice says, "Madrid also sympathizes with Cereza."

A woman speaks in Spanish while a female voice-over translates, "Of course we're excited, but we don't want to do it recklessly. We don't want to scare anyone away with our platform. Naturally, we'll respect the Constitution. We're well aware of what that's for." Then, a different woman says, "At a Podemos headquarters, they're not planning to take the policies of their Greek counterparts as a template, but they agreed."
A female voice says, "on some of their methods." A male voice then says, "scuole."

A man speaks, and simultaneously a woman's voice translates his speech into English: "We've been thinking here at Podemos about the kind of economic strategy that we should develop. We see that the differences are really significant, and we should probably take different strategies. But apart from that, one thing is really clear. Giving people the chance to express their will on big political and economic decisions publicly, such as via a referendum, is always a positive thing."
A woman says, "But Spain's ruling conservative..."

A female voice says, "party says Podemos is neither interested in democracy nor capable of governing. There are lots of these anti-political models in Europe that have no idea what they're doing. All they want is to use their power to erode democratic institutions. Right now, Greece's Syriza party is just the biggest example of this." This is accompanied by a male voice speaking simultaneously in Spanish.

A woman speaks in a clear voice, "Yet Podemos deputies take their work seriously, even if that's conducting civil marriages rather than reshaping society. Marta Gomez reckons she can only win people's trust by doing her job properly. After all, not all Spaniards agree with her about Greece's brinkmanship."
A female voice speaks, "Greece has to make some changes, but it's under too much pressure right now," amidst background conversation in Spanish.

A female voice speaks in Spanish, "Estoy a favor de Grecia," while another female voice says in English, "I support Greece, it shows the kind of courage no other country has." A male voice then speaks in Spanish, "A mí, por ejemplo, no me parece que," while another male voice says in English, "Greece is up to no good. It's not showing any respect towards other countries." The Spanish-speaking male voice continues, "de Europa, vamos."
After her day job, Martha Gomez holds an open-air town meeting in her own district.

A woman says, "to hear about the concerns in her community. They may be a long way from Athens, but Podemos supporters still feel a close connection with Greek people." This is followed by a man speaking in Spanish. The sound of a crowd chattering and applause is heard.

And I think there's there's, you know, heightened political sensitivity." Another man replies, "I yeah, I stole your stat. I think you probably heard that. But but we're down 500." This is all accompanied by background chatter.

A person speaks, "Yeah. Minimize. We're not down 100 points, Bill. 500 is still a significant number. Apple now down 10% from its highs, a number of stocks are down 5 and 6%. People are going to wonder why. What it can't just be history or natural selling. Don't you think there's some cause?" Another person responds, "No. I I just think it's the ebb and flow of the market. I think the fact that..." This is all accompanied by the murmur of a crowd.

A man speaks, "...in our stocks, because the market's been so stable the last year and sort of steadily higher, people's sensitivity, I think, to decline is probably greater. So it feels, it feels worse than it is. Usually over over the last 100 years, we've had, you know, several 5% drops in the market within one year, typically. So I think this is just trivial." Over the sound of background chatter, another man says, "Yeah, and Charles, you've been in the business..."

A person speaks in a clear voice, "is 50 years, okay? You you've read you've written 16 books. You've seen pretty much every kind of market cycle that we've had, but some would suggest that this time is different because you've got central banks with about 15 to 20 trillion dollars in holdings. You've got interest rates which were artificially depressed for so many years. Is there any historical precedent to the kind of market we see today?" This is accompanied by background chatter.

A man speaks, "ly not, but in the detail. But in the general thing that there's always terribly interesting things going on, very important trends being worked out, and really smart people paying attention trying to figure out what does that mean for prices in individual securities. It's the same old, same old, same old." Another man then asks, "No, what's what's the most important thing going on right now?" All of this is accompanied by the sound of a crowd murmuring in the background.
A man speaks, "what would you say for the macro market globally? Is it rates? Is it central bank involvement? Is it investor euphoria?" This is accompanied by indistinct background chatter.

A man speaks, "You asked a question, I have to tell you, I think the really most important thing going on is that retirement security is not being given the attention that it really needs because people are living longer than they ever did before and they don't understand how much money it takes to be financially okay during their retirement. That's really important. Honestly, the sorts of questions that you'd like me to get into, I have to tell you, for me, they are details." This is followed by another man speaking, "500 points is a significant move down though, Bill."

A man speaks, "and I think that I mean I hear your point Charles, definitely people want to retire. The markets has been certainly very strong. Given valuations, given rates, given Central Bank involvement, is the market in your mind particularly fragile right now?" A second man replies, "No. No, I don't think so. I mean I think you know, again, when you're when you're in these declines, if we go down 500 points for, you know, five more days in a row, uh you know, people get". Throughout the exchange, there is a low murmur of background chatter.

A man speaks, "increasingly agitated. And in the beginning of 2016, remember the market down 15% in the first six weeks. And then it rallied significantly the rest of the year. And all of the stuff that it was worried about that took it down 15%, macro worries about Russia, about about China, about the Fed tightening, all that proved to be just noise. And I think that right now, the most important thing that's going on in the market right now, I think, or in the world from a macro standpoint is global synchronized recovery. And I think that's the first time we've seen that in in many, many years. But earnings are going up, cash flows are going up, and you know, I think I think the greatest risk that people face in markets is is they they they fail to understand a very important thing, which is the economy almost always grows. And and earnings almost always go up. We have recessions and stocks go up most of the time. And so the risk to people's long-term financial health is being under-invested when in in long bull markets and not the the drops that they get in bear markets. Even in even with the crash of '87, the financial crisis of 2008. If people just stayed the course, they'd be fine." A woman then speaks, "Hey there, thanks for checking out CNBC on YouTube. Thanks for watching," accompanied by background music.

audio_captions: A series of swooshing sounds can be heard as a man speaks in an energetic voice, "The freakiest records people have set with their own bodies. The human body is capable of doing some amazing things. It can take a massive beating and stomach that burrito you got from the back of some fella's truck. Of course, that's just the tip of the human body's power."
An energetic male voice speaks, "And we're not talking about touching your nose with your tongue," accompanied by upbeat music.

A man speaks in a clear voice, "Or doing that party trick where Justin Trudeau throws himself down a flight of stairs unscathed." This is followed by a whooshing sound. He continues, "Get ready because here are eight freaky records people have set with their bodies." Another whooshing sound is heard. The man says, "Tongue piercings, unlike other piercings on the body, aren't exactly decorative." This is followed by a whooshing sound. He continues, "The tongue isn't as noticeable as say the ears or the nose." Another whooshing sound is heard. He concludes, "Yet there are people out there who have their taste buds poked and impaled for the sake of, mmm, fashion?"

A male speaker says, "The tongue isn't exactly the most spacious real estate on the human body, so there isn't a lot of room to work with. Enter Frank Vaca from Bellville, New Jersey, who's managed to fit 18 piercings on his tongue." A whooshing sound is heard. The speaker continues, "Frank is a bounty hunter who, from our best guess, has taken up the hobby of putting holes in his tongue because there's nothing else to do in Bellville, New Jersey." This is followed by another whooshing sound. The speaker then says, "Frank is actually looking into removing his piercings so he can space them out more efficiently and double the amount that he has now." The speech is accompanied by upbeat electronic music.

A male narrator speaks, "In fact, on January 13th, 2017, he live-streamed an extra two piercings to beat his own record of 16." He continues, "Without much metal in his mouth, he might as well get a silver tongue. We only have one question." This is all accompanied by upbeat, electronic background music.
A person asks, "How does he eat?" Another person speaks, "Many people get their ears pierced so they can wear fancy, fancy jewelry," accompanied by upbeat music.

A man speaks in an energetic, announcer-like voice, "But when everyone starts doing something, it becomes harder to stand out. That's why if you want the holes in your body to get noticed, you got to go big or go home. Kalaelo Kaiwi is a resident of Hawaii who has the largest known ear flesh tunnels. And that's a fancy way of saying he pierced and stretched his earlobes into oblivion. Officially measured on April 15, 2014, Kaiwi's earlobes measured in at 10.5 centimeters in diameter, which is roughly the same size as a teacup. A clenched fist could fit through those holes." Swoosh sound effects are heard between phrases, all set to a background of upbeat electronic music.

A male narrator speaks over upbeat electronic music, saying, "In addition to his massive ear hoops, Kaiwi also sports piercings, tattoos, subdermal horns, and a split tongue. But seriously, shouldn't he have the world record for closest resemblance to a demon? We're almost done with people who put holes inside their bodies, we promise."

A male voice speaks against a backdrop of upbeat music, saying, "When you can't beat out someone else's sheer size, the only thing to go for is quantity." A pop sound is heard, and the voice continues, "Joel Miggler is a 22-year-old man from Germany who has an astounding 11 flesh tunnels in his face. We should add that none of the holes in his face are accidental." A static burst is heard, followed by more speech: "Now, we're pretty sure most of us would rather protect ourselves from that kind of trauma, but Miggler embraces his uh rather incomplete look." Another static burst occurs, and the voice concludes, "Joel's body modifications, as he likes to refer to them, are scattered on his nose and lips. However, the largest ones are on his cheeks."

A character speaks, "The cheek windows, which offer a pretty unhindered view of his maw, measure at 34 mm, but he says he wants to expand them to 40 mm." A whooshing sound occurs, followed by more speech: "His girlfriend says she doesn't mind the holes at all and actually finds it rather unique. Uh, we guess Germans dig that whole Swiss cheese look." A sound of paper being handled is heard. The character continues, "And number four, we're giving you a look at this modern-day Pinocchio."

A character speaks, "However, there's no lying about just how big this schnoz is." A whooshing sound is heard, followed by more speech, "Mehmet Özyürek was born in Turkey in 1949 and is the proud owner of the largest nose in the world." This is all accompanied by upbeat music.
A male voice speaks, "Measured in Italy on March 18th, 2010, Özyürek's nose measures 8.8 cm from bridge to tip." This is all accompanied by light, upbeat background music.

Upbeat electronic music plays throughout. A male voice says, "We can only wonder what kind of superpowers come with such a large nose. Can he tell the words on a cake just by smelling it? How much Kleenex does he have to use when he has a cold?" A whooshing sound is heard, and a different male voice says, "Well, nobody knows for sure, but Mehmet Özyürek." Following another whooshing sound, the first voice says, "You know those scenes in cartoons where a pretty woman walks by and someone's eyes pop out of their head?" A popping sound is heard, and the voice continues, "You could probably guess where we're going with this one. Kim Goodman from the good old US of A is the world record holder for proptosis. That means she can displace her eyeballs and pop them out of her sockets at will."

A male voice speaks, "While the majority of us prefer to keep our eyes safely in their sockets." A popping sound is heard, followed by the voice continuing, "Kim Goodman can extend her eyeballs 12 millimeters. She discovered her talent one day when she was hit on the head with a hockey mask."

A man speaks enthusiastically, "Wow, I wonder what her eyes have seen to make them so ready to leave her head like that," followed by a whoosh sound. He continues, "For such a small part of the human body, the tongue sure is involved in a lot of world records," which is followed by a swoosh sound. He then says, "Nick Stoeberl from Salinas, California has the longest tongue in the entire world." This is all accompanied by upbeat music.

A male speaker says, "His tongue measures an impressive 10.1 cm from the tip to the top of his closed lip. However, most impressive of all is Nick's hobby and how he utilizes his tongue." This is accompanied by upbeat, synthesized music.

A man speaks in an energetic voice, "He actually makes works of art with his record-setting muscle, covering it in a layer of plastic wrap before dipping it in paints to create modern-day masterpieces." This is accompanied by upbeat electronic music.
A character says, "Bad Vincent," followed by a clicking sound.

A man speaks, "Bach never thought of that, now did he? Maybe you can get together with the tongue-piercing guy and they can collaborate." This is followed by a whoosh sound. The man continues, "Have you ever gone to a restaurant and ordered a giant triple-stacker burger, only to realize your bite is a little lacking?" Another whoosh sound is heard before he says, "We all know that feeling. Well, except for Bernard Schmidt." A whoosh sound plays, and he continues, "Bernard Schmidt from Germany is credited with having the largest gape of any living person, meaning he can open really wide." After another whoosh, he says, "How wide? His mouth measures an intense 8.8 centimeters at its widest, beating out the previous record by 4 millimeters." A whoosh is heard, and he goes on, "That may not sound very impressive, but just wait until you see him put an entire burger in his mouth." Following another whoosh, he states, "This guy makes a Big Mac look like a peanut butter and jelly sandwich." A final whoosh sound is heard, and he says, "Health magazines are obsessed with being thin." All of this is accompanied by upbeat background music.

A high-pitched male voice says, "According to magazines like Seventeen or Cosmopolitan, you ain't pretty unless your waistline is tiny." This is followed by a series of whoosh sound effects and upbeat, synthesized background music. A deep-voiced narrator then speaks, "Enter 79-year-old Cathie Jung, who has the smallest waistline in the world. Though it may not look like it, these pictures are 100% genuine. Since the age of 38, Cathie's love for Victoria-era clothing inspired her to wear a tight corset every day for 23 hours, only removing it when she showers. By constricting her body for nearly 24 hours a day for four decades, her waist shrunk to a paltry 15 inches."

A male voice speaks, "Kathy has never undergone any special diet or surgery. It's simply her love for Victorian-era clothing that landed her a world record." A whoosh sound is heard, and the voice continues, "Who knew the Victorians were still inspiring fashion trends?" Following another whoosh sound, the voice says, "With 7 billion people on this planet, we're sure there's some pretty freaky folks we missed." Upbeat background music plays throughout.

Upbeat electronic music plays as a male voice says, "What are some other eye-popping cringe-inducing records you've heard of?" A static-like sound effect occurs. The voice continues, "For everything shocking, astounding, and all around amazing, keep it tuned here." After the sound effect plays again, the voice says, "Don't forget to hit that subscribe button and join us again next time. See you later now."

A man says, "It's great to be here with you, Emery." A woman replies, "What did you bring with us?" The man then says, "Yeah, so we're."

A man speaks, "memorabilia with us to share with fans this weekend." This is accompanied by the sound of wooden bats lightly tapping against each other. The man continues, "Below that, we have a Charlie Gehringer bat. This is from 1934. Amazing. Below that, one of my personal favorites, a Pudge Rodriguez." The woman says, "Yes." The man adds, "And then we got an Alan Trammell bat." The woman exclaims, "Oh, yes." The man goes on, "So, it's gonna be really fun. Anyone can come up, they can put some gloves on, they can hold this." The woman says, "Wow." The man finishes, "And one of the the other cool things, we'll be uh shaping bats the old fashioned way uh at Tiger at Tiger." A woman says, "Oh."

A man says, "so uh the wood chips will be flying." A woman says, "I love that." The man continues, "You'll you'll see uh you'll see the guy with the tools shaping the bat. So it's going to be really amazing. And one of the great things is we're giving away free museum passes." A woman says, "All right."
A person speaks, "to anybody who comes up to us. Uh, we just want them to come down to Louisville and really experience this amazing..."

A man says, "museum that we have. Again, it's only a five and a half hour drive. There's lots to do in Louisville. Really wonderful place." A woman responds, "Right. Oh yeah, it's a nice family trip. And and that's what's so amazing."

A man speaks, "...just about the mobile museum but coming down to our museum. Um, it spans generations. That's the beauty of baseball. I mean, anybody can come up and recognize any of these players and just say..." A woman says, "Yes." The man continues, "...wow, like I want to hold, I want to hold the Pudge bat, I want to hold the, the Gehringer bat. Uh, and then, you know, it's the same with coming down to our museum. You can go on our award-winning factory tour and everyone who comes in, I have some mini bats up here. Anyone who comes in..."

A man speaks, "gets a free mini bat, and it's it's just a beautiful experience." A woman asks, "And you can personalize those too?" A thud is heard. The woman exclaims, "Oh my gosh!" The man says, "Look at that."

A man says, "That is that is beautiful. That has Anne-Marie's name on it right there. But let's let's see your pose." A woman replies, "Oh, my pose." The man continues, "Let's let's see that stance." The woman then says, "I play in a cheer."

A woman speaks, "softball game every year and if you saw my swing you would cry." A man replies, "Look at that." The woman enthusiastically continues, "But this is fantastic. This is so nice. A female speaker says, "That's fantastic. We'll put all the information on our website wxyz.com. Tiger Fest starts tomorrow." A male speaker says, "Yes." audio_captions: A male voice announces, "On this episode of China Uncensored."
A character speaks, "Hey, who turned off the internet?" A low piano chord plays.

A whoosh sound is followed by a click. A man speaks, "Nah, there you go. Hi, welcome to China Uncensored. I'm your host, Chris Chappell. You know, I remember a time when there was no internet and we didn't need it. In my day, when we wanted to look something up, we would just look up and hope that Zeus used a passing by cloud to communicate with us."

A male speaker with an energetic voice says, "When that didn't work, we would have to wait for a blind poet to incorporate the requested information into a 40-hour long epic poem. And if we were interested in someone, we didn't Facebook stalk them, we just stalked them. Got our exercise, too. But nowadays, just because 500 million people suddenly can't get online, everyone has a conniption. For several hours on January 21st, China's internet was down and people couldn't not get on blocked websites. Initial reports from state-run Xinhua said it could have been hackers behind the internet shutdown, but the real culprit was actually much more pathetic. Reuters reported they were told by..."
A man speaks, "anonymous sources familiar with the Chinese government's web management operations."
A person speaks, "that they were trying to make changes to the Great Firewall. That's China's pervasive internet censorship system that blocks..."

A man speaks in a clear voice, "websites. In doing so, they accidentally rerouted two-thirds of China's internet traffic to one of those blocked websites. I think we managed to get a picture of those internet technicians." He gives a soft chuckle and continues, "Who gave them that job? But the website, it was the worst website possible for a regime that likes to keep a tight grip on the internet. About one million requests per second."
A male voice says, "or sent to an internet address owned by Dynamic Internet Technology." A keyboard click is heard.

A man with a clear voice speaks, "a company that provides anti-censorship software specifically to Chinese internet users that allows them to get past the firewall. Not only that, but DIT's incredibly popular software Freegate, which has been used by internet users in other repressive regimes around the world like Iran, Egypt and Burma, and which I'm providing a link below, was created by Falun Gong practitioners, the spiritual practice that the Chinese regime has been trying oh so hard to wipe out. Here's what likely happened according to the experts. The Great Firewall blocks websites using something called DNS poisoning. DNS is like a directory for the internet. When you type in"
A person speaks, "youtube.com, it looks up YouTube's IP address, which looks like a string of numbers," followed by the sound of keyboard typing.

A person speaks, "and sends you there. Now, imagine you're trying to make a call to your friend, but then someone intercepted your phone call and sent you to a different phone number. That's what happens with DNS poisoning. Instead of connecting you to YouTube, the Great Firewall intercepts and redirects you to another website, essentially blocking you from getting to YouTube."
A voice says, "It looks like the sensor just made a mistake."

A character speaks in a clear, conversational voice, "And instead of redirecting traffic away from DIT's website, like it usually does, it redirected all of the traffic to the website. Oops. The sheer amount of traffic, however, meant that people were just seeing an error message. So, just to sum up..."
A person says, "in an effort to", followed by a click sound.
A male voice speaks, "troll the internet," followed by a click sound.
A person speaks, "Chinese censors accidentally".

A man speaks, "sent hundreds of millions of Chinese internet users to a website created by Falun Gong practitioners to beat Chinese censors. I could not make this stuff up. Now, before it came out that it was China's own government that was responsible for killing the internet,"
A person speaks, "There was a lot of speculation whether or not Falun Gong practitioners had hacked the Chinese internet."

Light background music plays as a man speaks in a clear voice: "This gave a lot of Western media the opportunity to blindly repost propaganda put out by the Chinese regime at face value. Like how Falun Gong practitioners once hacked into government TV satellite broadcasting systems in 2002. What was not mentioned was that it was to broadcast 'False Fire', a documentary that exposed the Tiananmen self-immolation, the hoax the Chinese regime used to justify the persecution of the spiritual practice, and that all six Falun Gong practitioners involved were captured, tortured, and are now currently dead. You can learn all about the immolation hoax on last week's episode, just click on the link." A mouse click sound is heard. "But so this makes me think. Falun Gong has been getting in the news a lot lately, but it seems like a lot of people still don't really know what it is or why it's being persecuted. So I don't know, do you want China Uncensored to cover it? Let me know in the comments section below and be sure to check out the Facebook page for more. It's been growing super fast lately and I want to thank all of you for your support. Once again, I'm Chris Chappell and this was China Uncensored." This is followed by a short musical outro.

We actually had to leave Matunuck Point because we realized if we didn't leave then, we wouldn't be able to leave. The road was flooding. So, this is Matunuck Beach Road right here, and you can get an idea of water flowing here, about six inches of water here, and if we go a half mile that way, you can't get out, it's blocked. audio_captions: A crowd of people shout. A man speaks, "The Omar al-Mukhtar battalion of the Free Syrian Army, vowing to drive Bashar al-Assad's forces from Idlib province. The video is unverified." People continue to shout. The man says, "On a cross-border visit to the Turkish city of Antakya, the battalion's commander, Ahmad al-Kanatri, Abu Hamza..."
A male voice says, "said the FSA is making big gains."
A man speaks, "in territory and manpower." Another man speaks in Arabic, followed by an English translation, "the number of defectors is now 100,000."

A male voice speaks, "And now they are defecting in bigger groups. This is a new phenomenon. The reason for the higher number of defections is that the regime is carrying out so many massacres every day." This is accompanied by the sound of indistinct background chatter.
A man speaks in a firm voice, "and the soldiers realize this regime must fall."

A man speaks in a clear voice, "Activists claim this video given to VOA shows stockpiles of weapons amassed by the rebel fighters. Abu Hamza denies Syrian government claims that foreign powers are arming what it calls the FSA terrorists. He says rebels need more."

A man speaks in Arabic, "نطالب ان يكون هناك حظر جوي." A second man speaks over him in English, "We need a no-fly zone. It's so important the world does this because Assad's jets are firing on unarmed people and targeting anything that moves. We have no way to protect ourselves." All of this is accompanied by the sound of shouting and commotion.
A man says, "Activists told VOA that some foreign weapons."
A person speaks, "are being taken over the border, but they refused to appear on camera." A different person then says, "Details of the meeting."
A man speaks, "and the deals done in this city are kept very quiet. But Antakya has become the main logistical headquarters for the opposition outside Syria." A siren wails in the background.
A man speaks, "Many FSA fighters are based at nearby refugee camps."
A character speaks, "like Yala doll."

A person speaks in Arabic, followed by another person speaking in English, "Armed defectors here announce their name, rank, and show their military ID. This fighter, an ethnic Turkmen, had just returned from fighting in Idlib province." A third person then says a short, unclear word.

A man speaks, "The FSA controls big parts of Syria. Actually, the Syrian government is really only in control of the center of big cities like Damascus, Aleppo, and inside Latakia. All around the cities, almost everywhere is under control of the FSA."
A crowd of people shouts, with one voice crying out, "Allahu Akbar!" This is followed by the sound of an explosion. A man's voice then states, "Reporting restrictions in Syria."
A male voice says, "means such claims are impossible to verify. But in recent days..." This is accompanied by the sound of something breaking.
A man says, "Fierce fighting has broken out in the heart of the Syrian capital. The FSA said Tuesday." This is accompanied by the sounds of explosions and gunfire.
A man speaks, "that the battle for the liberation of Damascus had begun." A crowd chants and claps. The man speaks again, "at Yada camp, buoyed by recent FSA advances."
A person speaks, "The refugees and fighters gather for an anti-Assad protest," accompanied by the sound of a crowd chanting.
A crowd of people can be heard shouting and chattering as a person speaks, "Children are thrust to the front. Most are too young to know the words."
A male voice speaks, "or their meaning, young lives."
A man speaks, "caught up in Syria's rapid descent into civil war. Henry Ridgwell for VOA News, Antakya, Turkey." The sounds of a crowd shouting and people wailing can be heard.
